There were 9 CRNMB events ( ), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 3.2% (95% CI, 1.7-6.0). Eight events occurred in patients who were anticoagulated with warfarin, and 1 occurred in a patient who was treated with rivaroxaban. High bleed–risk surgery (vs minimal/low/moderate) was associated with significantly greater odds of postoperative bleeding (composite of major bleeding + CRNMB: OR, 7.3; 95% CI, 1.5-35.4; P = .01). Similarly, undergoing a urologic or gynecologic procedure (vs all others) was also associated with substantially increased odds of postoperative bleeding (OR, 6.6; 95% CI, 1.8-24.5; P = .005). Postoperative microvascular APS occurred in 2 patients (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6). The first occurred on POD 10 in a triple-positive patient who developed biopsy-proven thrombotic microangiopathy of a transplanted kidney, which led to graft rejection. The second happened on POD 8 in another triple-positive patient and presented as an adrenal gland hemorrhage. Clinicians attributed this event to microvascular thrombosis and adrenal infarction, which subsequently led to adrenal insufficiency. This occurred in a 25-year-old triple-positive APS patient with ulcerative colitis who underwent a colonoscopy. On POD 8, the patient developed acalculous cholecystitis, adrenal hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia while receiving prophylactic tinzaparin at a dose of 4500 IU SQ daily. A heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) ELISA was positive (optical density OD, 1.6), but functional testing (serotonin release assay) was negative, confirming the absence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. This single event met the criteria for probable CAPS (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 1.4% (95% CI, 0.0-7.6) among triple-positive patients. There was 1 death during the 30-day follow-up (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0) that was attributed to fatal bleeding (outlined earlier). Discussion Data to guide the perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy for patients with thrombotic APS are limited. Herein, we report results from a single-center, retrospective cohort of anticoagulated adults with thrombotic APS who underwent a planned invasive procedure or surgery. Perioperative anticoagulation management was generally consistent with contemporary guideline-directed practice. The 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and ISTH-defined major bleeding were low and comparable with contemporary non-APS cohorts. CAPS, a recognized concern in the setting of anticoagulation withdrawal and surgical stress, was rare. Our findings suggest that contemporary perioperative anticoagulation strategies, when applied with individualized attention to thrombotic and bleeding risk, can be safely implemented in patients with APS. Perioperative management in our cohort followed a consistent framework that reflected both guideline-concordant practices and local practice patterns. Most VKA-treated patients received some form of parenteral bridging anticoagulation, reflecting the ACCP guideline designation of APS as a high thrombotic–risk condition for which bridging may be appropriate. Concurrent antiplatelet therapy was uncommon (∼13%), and complicating perioperative thrombocytopenia was rare (4.3%). Few patients had a higher INR target (2.5-3.5; ∼5%). Holding warfarin for 5 days before surgery led to INR normalization (INR < 1.5) in most (∼92.6%) VKA-treated patients. In a previous single-center APS surgical cohort, guideline-concordant periprocedural anticoagulation management was associated with fewer thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications (7% vs 33%; OR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02-0.81; P = .04), and an INR of ≤1.5 at surgery was associated with fewer major bleeding events (6% vs 29%; OR, 0.19; 95% CI, 0.02-0.98; P = .05). The 30-day risks for major bleeding (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6) and CRNMB (3.2%; 95% CI, 1.7-6.0) compared favorably with those of contemporary non-APS cohorts. The 30-day risks for major bleeding in the BRIDGE trial were 1.3% and 3.2% in the nonbridging and bridging arms, respectively, whereas the risks ranged from 0.9% to 1.9% in the PAUSE study depending on the DOAC in question. , Importantly, in our study, major bleeding events were attributed to anatomic and procedural factors rather than anticoagulation status at bleeding onset. Most bleeding events occurred after a high bleed–risk procedure, including both of the recorded major bleeding events, and more than half of the bleeding events involved urologic or gynecologic procedures (renal biopsy, hysterectomy, transurethral resection of bladder tumor, uterine ablation). Few early bleeding events occurred during therapeutic-dose bridging; most occurred after appropriate perioperative interruption with INR values within the expected range at surgery. In contrast, delayed CRNMB events typically occurred after discontinuation of bridging during warfarin therapy with INRs within the therapeutic range (ie, not supratherapeutic), suggesting that these

anatomic and procedural factors rather than anticoagulation status at bleeding onset. Most bleeding events occurred after a high bleed–risk procedure, including both of the recorded major bleeding events, and more than half of the bleeding events involved urologic or gynecologic procedures (renal biopsy, hysterectomy, transurethral resection of bladder tumor, uterine ablation). Few early bleeding events occurred during therapeutic-dose bridging; most occurred after appropriate perioperative interruption with INR values within the expected range at surgery. In contrast, delayed CRNMB events typically occurred after discontinuation of bridging during warfarin therapy with INRs within the therapeutic range (ie, not supratherapeutic), suggesting that these delayed events were not directly attributable to bridging. Taken together, these findings underscore the importance of carefully considering the type of procedure (eg, urologic procedures) and postoperative bleeding risk when devising a perioperative anticoagulation management plan. Data from non-APS populations indicate that bridging increases postoperative bleeding without clearly reducing the thromboembolism risk, but these studies enrolled patients with lower-risk indications (eg, atrial fibrillation) and may not be generalizable to APS. , APS is both clinically and biologically heterogeneous. More than half of our cohort met Miyakis category I criteria, one-quarter were triple-positive, and moderate to high aPL titers were observed across multiple isotypes. These features typically indicate a higher thrombotic risk. Our cohort also demonstrated a substantial burden of clinical thrombotic risk factors. More than half had a previous ATE, the majority had a history of VTE, and nearly one-third had a concurrent autoimmune disease. Clinicians seemed to incorporate APS-related thrombotic risk into their perioperative decision-making. Patients with triple-positive APS and those with a previous ATE were more likely to receive therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging. Our findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all approach is unlikely to be appropriate in APS. Tailoring perioperative anticoagulation management to both APS-related thrombotic risk and procedural bleed risk seems to have been both feasible and safe in this heterogeneous, higher-risk cohort. Postoperative bridging in our cohort frequently comprised prophylactic-dose LMWH after high bleed–risk procedures; this may, in part, represent local extrapolation of postoperative dose modulation concepts that have been evaluated in other high thrombotic–risk populations (eg, patients with a mechanical heart valve), recognizing that therapeutic-dose anticoagulation in the immediate postoperative period is a shared driver of major bleeding risk. Given the observational design and low event counts, this practice pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Both ATE events occurred while patients were receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis. Microvascular events were uncommon overall (0.7%) but occurred exclusively in triple-positive patients; 1 event met the criteria for probable CAPS, which happened while the patient was receiving postoperative prophylactic LMWH. Although definitive causal inferences cannot be made, these observations, together with published case reports describing rapid, severe thrombotic events in triple-positive secondary APS (often with concomitant systemic autoimmune disease) after brief warfarin interruption despite LMWH bridging, supports considering therapeutic-dose bridging and tightly timed periprocedural anticoagulation strategies that minimize time off anticoagulation in the highest-risk phenotypes (ie, triple-positive APS and/or previous ATE). Conversely, for lower-risk phenotypes and/or higher bleed–risk procedures, initiating prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation early in the postoperative period with escalation as surgical hemostasis permits may offer a pragmatic balance. Prospective studies are needed to confirm optimal strategies across APS phenotypes. This study has several strengths. To our knowledge, it represents the largest, single-center cohort that evaluated perioperative anticoagulation management in patients with thrombotic APS. Perioperative antithrombotic strategies at our center followed relatively standardized workflows, enabling detailed characterization of warfarin interruption intervals, preoperative INR assessment, vitamin K use, LMWH bridging dose and timing, and postoperative VKA resumption practices. The outcome definitions adhered to widely recognized international standards, and the cohort encompassed a broad mix of invasive procedures with more than one-third classified as high bleed–risk procedures. TOH is the regional referral center for thrombosis, APS, and stroke, and patients with APS undergo close, frequent monitoring, including regular pharmacist-specialist contacts for VKA management. Consequently, although retrospective analyses are inherently susceptible to variable documentation and information bias, the likelihood of missing major thrombotic or bleeding outcomes is low. Important limitations should also be acknowledged. First, the measurement of aPL antibodies is itself a known challenge; our cohort spanned a period during which laboratory methodology transitioned from ELISA to CLIA platforms. Although we harmonized titers using published ISTH conversion thresholds and applied a 99th percentile positivity cutoff, some misclassification remains possible. Second, several patients underwent multiple perioperative interruptions, which led to more interruptions than there were patients. Although GEE models were used to account for within-patient clustering when evaluating bridging patterns and overall bleeding risk, events were too few to support multivariable modelling of clinical outcomes. Thus, the determined estimates and their CIs should be interpreted cautiously. Third, serial postoperative INR trajectories were not uniformly available across interruption episodes, precluding estimation of time spent below therapeutic range and time to reattain a therapeutic INR after warfarin resumption.

Second, several patients underwent multiple perioperative interruptions, which led to more interruptions than there were patients. Although GEE models were used to account for within-patient clustering when evaluating bridging patterns and overall bleeding risk, events were too few to support multivariable modelling of clinical outcomes. Thus, the determined estimates and their CIs should be interpreted cautiously. Third, serial postoperative INR trajectories were not uniformly available across interruption episodes, precluding estimation of time spent below therapeutic range and time to reattain a therapeutic INR after warfarin resumption. Fourth, concomitant hydroxychloroquine use was not systematically captured, limiting assessment of its potential influence on perioperative thrombotic and bleeding outcomes. Finally, as a retrospective, single-center analysis, perioperative decisions, including bridging intensity, were not protocolized and event counts were low, leading to wide confidence intervals for the event estimates. In summary, patients with thrombotic APS who underwent planned interruption of anticoagulation at our center experienced low 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and major bleeding when managed using contemporary perioperative strategies. Clinical practice patterns reflected a risk-adapted approach. Clinicians used therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging more often in patients with triple-positive APS or a history of ATE. They used prophylactic-dose bridging more frequently after high bleed–risk procedures. Individualized management that integrates APS-related thrombotic risk, procedural bleed risk, and clinical context seems safe. The occurrence of microvascular APS manifestations, including 1 case of probable CAPS, underscores that high-risk phenotypes remain vulnerable during anticoagulation withdrawal and merit heightened vigilance. Future research should focus on multicenter prospective studies to refine risk stratification, define optimal bridging strategies across APS phenotypes, and better characterize clinical outcomes in the perioperative setting. chunks.content: Introduction Myelofibrosis (MF) is a clonal hematologic malignancy that may arise de novo (primary MF, PMF) or evolve secondary to polycythemia vera (PV) or essential thrombocythemia (ET). It is characterized by progressive bone marrow fibrosis (BMF), peripheral cytopenias, splenomegaly, elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, and a constellation of burdensome constitutional symptoms, including fatigue, pruritus, night sweats, and weight loss [ ]. Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, remains the standard first-line therapy due to its demonstrated superiority over placebo or best available therapy in reducing splenomegaly and improving symptom burden [ ]. However, Ruxolitinib has several limitations. Hematologic toxicity, particularly anemia and thrombocytopenia, is common and mechanistically linked to the JAK-STAT pathway’s role in erythropoietin and thrombopoietin signaling. Moreover, Ruxolitinib has minimal impact on altering disease progression or preventing leukemic transformation to myeloproliferative neoplasm-blast phase (MPN-BP), and a substantial proportion of patients eventually exhibit suboptimal responses or discontinue therapy due to cytopenias [ ]. These therapeutic gaps have prompted the investigation of novel agents targeting alternative pathogenic pathways beyond JAK-STAT, including epigenetic regulators, apoptotic machinery, aberrant signaling cascades, and malignant stem cell populations. Several such agents—such as Navitoclax, Pelabresib, and Panobinostat—are being evaluated in combination with Ruxolitinib in ongoing clinical trials [ , ]. However, the current evidence base consists primarily of early-phase, single-arm studies with small cohorts, and few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or direct comparative studies exist. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to synthesize the available evidence on Ruxolitinib-based combination therapies for both primary and secondary MF, evaluating their efficacy and safety profiles to inform future clinical decision-making and research directions. Methods The recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were used to formulate the eligibility criteria for the systematic review and meta-analysis [ ]. Literature search/search strategy Databases (PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, LILACS, CNKI, WANFANG, VIP, CBM) and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to August 1, 2025, using terms: “Primary Myelofibrosis”, “Myelofibroses”, “Ruxolitinib”, “Jakavi”, “Combination therapy”, “Combination treatment”, using strategy: ((((Myelofibrosis) or (Myelofibroses)) and ((Ruxolitinib) or (Jakavi))) and ((Combination therapy) or (Combination treatment))). Reference lists of relevant reviews were screened. Outcomes and study selection/literature inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria: (1) Prospective/retrospective studies; (2) Patients with PMF or post-PV/ET MF; (3) Ruxolitinib-based combination therapy (e.g. with Selinexor, Pelabresib, BMS-986158); (4) Reported efficacy endpoints: SVR35 (≥35% spleen volume reduction or >50% spleen length reduction by palpation at 24 weeks), TSS50, JAK2V617F allele burden reduction, ≥1 grade bone marrow fibrosis improvement, hemoglobin response (≥1.5 g/dL increase from baseline without transfusions). Exclusion criteria: (1) <5 patients; (2) Non-Chinese/English publications; (3) Reviews, comments, case reports, preclinical studies, poor quality, or duplicate reports. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts, resolving disagreements with a third reviewer. Data extraction Two reviewers independently extracted data: first author, year, country, design, NCT ID, follow-up, disease status, sample size, age, sex, treatment, efficacy outcomes (SVR35, TSS50, etc.), and adverse events (AEs) graded by CTCAE v5.0. Latest follow-up data were preferred. Quality assessment and bias risk assessment The MINORS tool [ ] was used; most studies were of moderate quality. We assessed the publication bias of SVR35 and TSS50 in MF patients who received Ruxolitinib-based combination regimens using Egger’s tests conducted with Stata 15. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by sequentially eliminating each study from the pooled results. Statistical analysis Pooled proportions (P) and 95% CIs were calculated using the generic inverse variance method in RevMan 5.4. Standard errors (SE) were derived from proportions. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and I 2 statistics (fixed-effects model if I 2 <50%; random-effects otherwise). Subgroup analyses were performed based on combination drug and prior JAK inhibitor exposure. Results Search results/outcomes of the search process A total of 1,937 potentially eligible articles were initially identified through searches of multiple databases and supplementary sources. After removing duplicates using EndNote X9, 1,291 unique articles remained. Screening of these articles by title and abstract identified 63 for full-text review. Ultimately, 19 prospective studies met all predefined inclusion criteria and were included in the final meta-analysis. Collectively, these studies evaluated efficacy and safety outcomes in 1,088 patients. The literature selection process is depicted in . Among the 19 studies, Ruxolitinib and Selinexor combination therapy was used in 2 study [ , ], Panobinostat and Ruxolitinib in 2 studies [ , ], Pelabresib and Ruxolitinib in 3 studies [ ], Navitoclax and Ruxolitinib in 3 studies [ ], Pegylated Interferon Alfa 2a (IFNα) and Ruxolitinib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and 5-Azacitidine (AZA) in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Vismodegibin 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Sonidegib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Siremadlin in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Parsaclisib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Buparlisib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib, Nilotinib and Prednisone in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and

study [ , ], Panobinostat and Ruxolitinib in 2 studies [ , ], Pelabresib and Ruxolitinib in 3 studies [ ], Navitoclax and Ruxolitinib in 3 studies [ ], Pegylated Interferon Alfa 2a (IFNα) and Ruxolitinib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and 5-Azacitidine (AZA) in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Vismodegibin 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Sonidegib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Siremadlin in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Parsaclisib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and Buparlisib in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib, Nilotinib and Prednisone in 1 study [ ], Ruxolitinib and BMS-986158 in 1 study [ ]. In the study on combination therapy of Ruxolitinib and Buparlisib, Group A comprised JAK inhibitor–naïve MF patients, and Group B included patients who had previously received JAK inhibitors. For the purpose of this analysis, these cohorts were treated as two separate single-arm studies [ ]. presents a detailed summary of the clinical characteristics, treatment regimens, and primary outcomes of the included studies. Quality assessment and bias risk assessment Nineteen studies were carefully reviewed against the evaluation criteria from the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) [ ]. Except for items V and VIII ( ), the majority of the criteria received a 2-point rating, indicating moderate overall quality across the studies. Efficacy Data on spleen volume reduction of ≥ 35% (referred to as SVR35) or spleen length reduction >50% by palpation at 24 weeks, a total symptom score reduction of ≥ 50%(TSS50), reduction of JAK allele burden, ≥1 grade improvement of myelofibrosis and hemoglobin response were extracted from 19 articles. Since this analysis mixes early-phase studies, single-arm trials, and dose-finding analysis: such heterogeneity methodologically inappropriate for generating pooled effect measures. Therefore, we will directly conduct subgroup analyses in the following text. Subgroup analysis of different combination therapy drugs We also conducted subgroup analyses of SVR35 and TSS50 based on drugs combined with Ruxolitinib, dividing SVR35 into 13 subgroups of combination therapy and TSS50 into 8 subgroups. Subgroup analysis showed that two studies reported on Selinexor and Ruxolitinib combination therapy, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 65% (95% CI: 13–118%), while the pooled TSS50 ( ) was 54% (95% CI: 11–98%). Three studies reported on Pelabresib and Ruxolitinib combination therapy, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 51% (95% CI: 21–81%, I 2 = 98%), while the pooled TSS50 ( ) was 49% (95% CI: 38–59%, I 2 = 73%). Two studies reported on Panobinostat and Ruxolitinib combination therapy, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 51% (95% CI: 27–75%, I 2 = 67%), while the pooled TSS50 ( ) was 25% (95% CI: 1–49%), which was not statistically significant. Three studies reported on Navitoclax and Ruxolitinib combination therapy, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 46% (95% CI: 16–76%, I 2 = 96%), while the pooled TSS50 ( ) was 25% (95% CI: 18–32%, I 2 = 0%). One study reported on Sonidegib and Ruxolitinib combination therapy, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 44% (95% CI: 26–63%), while the pooled TSS50 ( Figure 2S ) was 42% (95% CI: 28–56%). Besides, one article each reported the combination therapy of BMS-986158 and Ruxolitinib, Nilotinib, Prednisone and Ruxolitinib, IFNα and Ruxolitinib, 5-AZA and Ruxolitinib, indicating that the pooled SVR35 was 90% (95% CI: 71–109%), 75% (95% CI: 45–105%), 70% (95% CI: 56–85%) and 58% (95% CI: 43–73%), respectively. Other effect results can be seen in . Additionally, multiple studies have shown that the combination regimens lead to a decrease of the JAK2V617F allele burden [ , , ], a decrease in myelofibrosis grade [ , , , ] and an improvement in anemia [ , ] For example, Ruxolitinib combined with Siremadlin, Panobinoatat and Pelabresib resulted in a decrease of the JAK2V617F allele burden, suggesting the clearance of tumor clones. The combination regimens of Ruxolitinib with Panobinoatat, Pelabresib and Naxitoclax promoted a decrease in myelofibrosis grade, suggesting the improvement in fibrosis. Ruxolitinib combined with Pelabresib and Naxitoclax helped to improve anemia. Subgroup analysis of different prior treatment According to whether patients had previously received JAK inhibitor treatment, the study was divided into two subgroups: JAK inhibitor–naïve patients and JAK inhibitor–treated patients. In the study evaluating the combination of Buparlisib and Ruxolitinib, Group A consisted of JAK inhibitor–naïve MF patients, while Group B included JAK inhibitor-treated MF patients. Therefore, this study was treated as two separate single-arm studies. Four studies explicitly excluded patients who had been treated with Ruxolitinib. Given that Ruxolitinib is the standard first-line treatment for myelofibrosis (MF), these four studies were temporarily categorized as involving JAK inhibitor–naïve patients. Eleven studies reported SVR35 outcomes ( ), and six studies reported TSS50 outcomes ( ) for JAK inhibitor–naïve MF patients, yielding pooled response rates of 65% (95% CI: 57–72%,

inhibitor–treated patients. In the study evaluating the combination of Buparlisib and Ruxolitinib, Group A consisted of JAK inhibitor–naïve MF patients, while Group B included JAK inhibitor-treated MF patients. Therefore, this study was treated as two separate single-arm studies. Four studies explicitly excluded patients who had been treated with Ruxolitinib. Given that Ruxolitinib is the standard first-line treatment for myelofibrosis (MF), these four studies were temporarily categorized as involving JAK inhibitor–naïve patients. Eleven studies reported SVR35 outcomes ( ), and six studies reported TSS50 outcomes ( ) for JAK inhibitor–naïve MF patients, yielding pooled response rates of 65% (95% CI: 57–72%, I 2 = 69%) and 52% (95% CI: 43–61%, I 2 = 53%), respectively. In comparison, six studies reported SVR35 ( ) and four studies reported TSS50 ( ) for JAK inhibitor–treated MF patients, with pooled response rates of 22% (95% CI: 11–32%, I 2 = 82%) and 26% (95% CI: 15–37%, I 2 = 77%), respectively. Among various combination regimens used in treatment-naïve patients, the combination of Selinexor with Ruxolitinib demonstrated the highest efficacy, with an SVR35 ( ) of 92% (95% CI: 76–107%) and a TSS50 ( ) of 78% (95% CI: 51–105%). The combination of BMS-986158 and Ruxolitinib achieved an SVR35 ( ) of 90% (95% CI: 71–109%), although symptom response data were not available. IFNα combined with Ruxolitinib yielded an SVR35 ( ) of 70% (95% CI: 56–85%). Pelabresib combined with Ruxolitinib yielded an SVR35 ( ) of 66% (95% CI: 61–72%, I 2 = 0%) and a TSS50 ( ) of 53% (95% CI: 48–59%, I 2 = 0%). In JAK inhibitor-treated patients, the combination of Siremadlin and Ruxolitinib showed relatively higher efficacy, with an SVR35 ( ) of 45% (95% CI: 16–75%). Selinexor combined with Ruxolitinib in this subgroup achieved an SVR35 ( ) of 38% (95% CI: 17–59%) and a TSS50 ( ) of 33% (95% CI: 16–51%). Other effect sizes are presented in . Subgroup analysis of different mechanisms of combination therapy drugs According to the types of drugs combined with Ruxolitinib, there are ten categories: HDAC inhibitors, BET inhibitors, Bcl-2 inhibitors, Hedgehog inhibitors, PI3K inhibitors, Hyomethylating agents, Interferon, XPO1 inhibitors, MDM2 inhibitors, and Tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Among them, research on XPO1 inhibitors includes two studies of Selinexor combined with Ruxolitinib, with an SVR35 of 65% (95% CI: 13–118%) and a TSS50 of 54% (95% CI: 11–98%). Research on BET inhibitors includes three studies of Pelabresib combined with Ruxolitinib and one study of BMS-986158 combined with Ruxolitinib, showing good efficacy, with an SVR35 of 60% (95% CI: 33–87%, I 2 = 97%) and a TSS50 of 49% (95% CI: 38–59%, I 2 = 73%). Research on HDAC inhibitors includes two studies of Panobinostat combined with Ruxolitinib, with an SVR35 of 51% (95% CI: 27–75%, I 2 = 67%) and a TSS50 of 25% (95% CI: 1–49%). Research on Bcl-2 inhibitors includes three studies of Navitoclax combined with Ruxolitinib, with an SVR35 of 46% (95% CI: 16–76%, I 2 = 96%) and a TSS50 of 25% (95% CI: 18–32%, I 2 = 0%). Research on Hedgehog inhibitors combined with Ruxolitinib includes one article on Vismodegib combined with Ruxolitinib and one article on Sonidegib combined with Ruxolitinib, with a pooled SVR35 of 40% (95% CI: 24–56%, I 2 = 0%) and a TSS50 of 40% (95% CI: 27–52%, I 2 = 0%). Additionally, one article each reported combination therapies of Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Interferon, Hyomethylating agents, and MDM2 inhibitors with Ruxolitinib, indicating that the pooled SVR35 ( ) was 75% (95% CI: 45–105%), 70% (95% CI: 56–85%), 58% (95% CI: 43–73%), and 45% (95% CI: 16–75%), respectively. The remaining effect results are shown in . Toxicity Pooled results of grade 3/4 AEs between different combination therapy The adverse events (AE) are mainly hematological AEs. Common hematological AEs included thrombocytopenia, anemia, and neutropenia. Subgroup analysis of hematological adverse events was conducted based on JAK inhibitor treatment status. In JAK inhibitor–naïve patients, the pooled rates of grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia ( ) and anemia ( ) were 17% (95% CI: 12–23%, I 2 = 51%) and 29% (95% CI: 20–38%, I 2 = 74%), respectively. In JAK inhibitor–treated patients, the corresponding rates were 34% (95% CI: 19–49%, I 2 = 90%) and 28% (95% CI: 16–39%, I 2 = 79%). Additionally, significant non-hematological AEs were reported, including nausea, vomiting, pneumonia, diarrhea, rash, weakness, fatigue, hypoxia, dyspnea, falls, elevated ALT and AST levels, and hypocalcemia. Publication bias We assessed the publication bias of SVR35 and TSS50 in MF patients who received Ruxolitinib-based combination regimens using Egger’s tests conducted with Stata 15. Evidence of publication bias was found after pooling the odds ratio (OR) assessments from all included studies, likely due to the relatively small sample sizes of the individual studies (SVR35: Egger’s test p = 0.013; TSS50: Egger’s

I 2 = 90%) and 28% (95% CI: 16–39%, I 2 = 79%). Additionally, significant non-hematological AEs were reported, including nausea, vomiting, pneumonia, diarrhea, rash, weakness, fatigue, hypoxia, dyspnea, falls, elevated ALT and AST levels, and hypocalcemia. Publication bias We assessed the publication bias of SVR35 and TSS50 in MF patients who received Ruxolitinib-based combination regimens using Egger’s tests conducted with Stata 15. Evidence of publication bias was found after pooling the odds ratio (OR) assessments from all included studies, likely due to the relatively small sample sizes of the individual studies (SVR35: Egger’s test p = 0.013; TSS50: Egger’s test p = 0.210; Reduction in JAK allele burden: Egger’s test p = 0.484; ≥1-grade improvement in myelofibrosis: Egger’s test p = 0.373; Hemoglobin response, Egger’s test p = 0.505). Sensitivity analyses Sensitivity analyses were conducted by sequentially eliminating each study from the pooled results, revealing that the combined findings are adequately robust. Discussion This meta-analysis of 19 trials involving 1,088 patients provides comparative efficacy and safety data on Ruxolitinib-based combination therapies in myelofibrosis (MF). In the absence of head-to-head trials, our findings suggest the following: Ruxolitinib + XPO1 Inhibitor (Selinexor) This combination demonstrated satisfactory efficacy, particularly in JAK inhibitor–naïve patients (SVR35 92%, TSS50 78%), while still maintaining benefit in previously treated patients (SVR35 38%, TSS50 33%). Selinexor exerts its effects by inhibiting XPO1, thereby impacting multiple MF-related pathways, including STAT, ERK, and AKT signaling [ ]. In preclinical investigations of MF, synergistic activity has been observed between Selinexor and Ruxolitinib, consistent with our conclusion and suggesting the potential for SEL as a backbone for novel treatment combinations for MF [ ]. However, limited safety data and only two studies necessitate further validation. Ruxolitinib + BET inhibitors (Pelabresib, BMS-986158) This regimen showed high efficacy in treatment-naïve patients (Pelabresib: SVR35 66%, TSS50 53%; BMS-986158: SVR35 90%). BET inhibitors interfere with epigenetic regulation and have demonstrated synergistic effects with JAK inhibitors in preclinical models [ ]. Efficacy of pelabresib was reduced in previously treated patients (SVR35 20%, TSS50 37%). Pooled analysis of the BET inhibitor group supports a strong overall efficacy profile (SVR35 60%, TSS50 49%). Pelabresib additionally improved fibrosis grade, anemia, and decreased allele burden. Currently, a clinical trial led by Claire N Harrison is underway, aiming to investigate whether Pelabresib in combination with Ruxolitinib will result in improved efficacy outcomes compared with Ruxolitinib in combination with placebo [ ]. Regarding the efficacy and safety of the combined treatment of Pelabresib and Ruxolitinib, more answers will be available in the future. Other combinations in JAK inhibitor-naïve patients Ruxolitinib combined with IFN-α (SVR35 70%), Navitoclax (Bcl-2 inhibitor: SVR35 62%, TSS50 31%), 5-azacitidine (Hyomethylating agent, SVR35 58%), Buparlisib (PI3K inhibitor, SVR35 55%), and Panobinostat (HDAC inhibitor, SVR35 51%) showed varying degrees of efficacy, though generally lower than XPO1i or BETi combinations. Data on efficacy in previously treated patients were limited or less favorable. Not recommended Combinations with Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (Sonidegib, Vismodegib) and the PI3K inhibitor Parsaclisib demonstrated low SVR35 rates (36–44% and 26%, respectively), with no clear evidence of improved efficacy over Ruxolitinib monotherapy. These combinations are unlikely to warrant further development in MF. Prior JAK inhibitor exposure Across most combinations, efficacy was significantly greater in JAK inhibitor–naïve patients. Among previously treated patients, combinations with Selinexor, Siremadlin (MDM2 inhibitor: SVR35 45%), and the triple regimen of Ruxolitinib/nilotinib/prednisone (SVR35 75% in a mixed treatment-status cohort) appeared most promising; however, the number of cases was small, with only eight patients assessed for spleen length. Currently, there are relatively few combination therapies for MF patients exposed to JAK2 inhibitors, and further exploration is needed in the future. Safety Hematologic adverse events were predominant, with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia being the most common. Anemia rates were highest with Panobinostat (49%) and Siremadlin (48%), while thrombocytopenia was most frequent with Siremadlin (48%) and Navitoclax (43%). Notably, combinations involving XPO1 and BET inhibitors showed relatively lower hematologic toxicity; for example, Selinexor was associated with a thrombocytopenia rate of just 7%. Non-hematologic AEs were frequently observed but varied widely across studies. Limitations The analysis is constrained by small sample sizes per combination regimen, a small number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), limited data on long-term outcomes (e.g. progression-free survival, overall survival), and absence of direct comparative trials. The potential for publication bias must also be acknowledged. Conclusion While Ruxolitinib remains the standard treatment for MF, its limitations in disease modification and long-term efficacy highlight the need for novel therapeutic strategies. Ruxolitinib-based combination regimens offer improved clinical responses and the potential for more meaningful disease control. The optimal regimen should be individualized based on disease characteristics and prior treatment history. Efficacy is highly influenced by prior JAK inhibitor exposure. Future research should prioritize large-scale RCTs, evaluation of long-term outcomes, head-to-head comparisons, and the optimal timing and sequencing of combination strategies.

documents.title: ASH 2020 Guidelines for Sickle Cell Disease Management of Acute Chronic Pain

chunks.content: Introduction Sickle cell anemia (SCA) is one of the most common genetic disorders worldwide, with newborns in Nigeria accounting for 50% of all affected newborns, amounting to 150 000 cases annually. , Children with SCA in sub-Saharan Africa face higher mortality rates compared with children in high-resource settings. , , Malnutrition in children with SCA further compounds this problem and increases the risk of hospitalization and death. , Malnutrition is prevalent and likely one of the most common causes of death in children with SCA living in Africa. , , , , , In Nigeria, only 20% of all children aged <5 years with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) receive treatment. Moreover, there are no evidence-based guidelines for treating malnutrition in children aged ≥5 years or children of any age with SCA, , although the prevalence of growth faltering increases with age in children with SCA. , , The lack of evidence-based guidelines for managing SAM in children with SCA in Nigeria, and other sub-Saharan African regions where both malnutrition and SCA are prevalent, , is a major public health challenge. Furthermore, there is biological plausibility for improving nutritional status to decrease the morbidity and mortality due to SCA. Several preclinical studies in mice with sickle cell disease (SCD) have provided strong evidence of nutritional interventions to improve the health of the offspring, increase bone health, and decrease inflammatory vasculopathy. , , , Furthermore, in a phase 3 randomized controlled trial, L-glutamine, an amino acid, compared with placebo, reduced the incidence of painful vaso-occlusive events in children and adults with SCA. These data demonstrate the potential importance of identifying and treating SAM in children with SCA. Hydroxyurea therapy is a potentially unique addition to treating malnutrition in children with SCA. Hydroxyurea has multiple benefits for children with SCA, such as reducing morbidity from vaso-occlusive episodes, acute chest syndrome, and strokes while also improving hemoglobin (Hb) levels. , Lower Hb levels are associated with decreased weight-for-age, height-for-age, and body mass index (BMI) z scores. , , Although some studies suggest that hydroxyurea has no adverse effects on growth and may even have a positive impact, , , , , there is currently no randomized controlled trial testing whether hydroxyurea can directly improve growth as a primary hypothesis. The absence of evidence-based malnutrition guidelines for children with SCA is a public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, where poverty, the high number of children with SCA, and the prevalence of SAM are pressing issues. , To address this critical knowledge gap, we conducted the first National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded trial to treat SAM (BMI z score of <−3.0) in children aged from 5 to 12 years with SCA in Nigeria (SAMS trial; NCT03634488 ). Methods Study design The SAMS trial was a multicenter, open-label, feasibility randomized controlled trial ( NCT03634488 ) conducted in Kano, Nigeria. The study protocol is presented in . Participants who were eligible were assigned in a 1:1 ratio based on a permuted block allocation scheme, block sizes of 2 and 4, stratified based on the sex, within the clinical site, to receipt of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) alone or with hydroxyurea at a fixed dose (20 mg/kg per day). Ethical review of the study Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional review boards of Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, Murtala Mohammed Specialist Hospital, and the Vanderbilt University Medical Center. The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control in Nigeria provided regulatory approval. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) reviewed the study progress and adverse events (AEs). Written informed consent and assent for children aged >7 years were obtained before screening and enrollment. Children whose caregivers declined enrollment in the study received standard care. The SAMS trial was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Study participants Children receiving care at the 2 study sites, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital and Murtala Mohammed Specialist Hospital, were evaluated for study eligibility. The inclusion criteria for children with SCA were as follows: (1) laboratory diagnosis of SCA (HbSS or HbSB 0 thalassemia), (2) SAM defined as a BMI z score of <−3.0, (3) age between 5.00 and 12.99 years, and (4) residence within a 2-hour driving distance from the medical center. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) children with complicated SAM; (2) children with electrolyte disturbances at baseline; (3) children on disease-modifying therapy (hydroxyurea or regular blood transfusion therapy); (4) children enrolled in other studies; (5) children with diabetes and other chronic illnesses; (6) children with known HIV infection; and (7) children with known allergies to dairy or peanuts. Children with complicated acute SAM (including, but not limited to, poor appetite, altered mental status, fever, other signs of infection, bilateral edema of the extremities, or respiratory distress) were excluded and referred for inpatient treatment. Children with complicated acute SAM (including, but not limited to, poor appetite, altered mental status, fever, other signs of infection, bilateral edema of the extremities, or respiratory distress) were excluded and referred for inpatient treatment. To improve the adherence to the RUTF and decrease sharing among household members, siblings aged from 5 to 12 years with SAM but without SCA were eligible for screening and RUTF therapy. Interventions Hydroxyurea is an antimetabolite chemotherapy drug approved by National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control in Nigeria to prevent acute vaso-occlusive pain and other complications in SCA. Children with SCA randomly assigned to the treatment arm received moderate fixed-dose hydroxyurea therapy at 20 mg/kg per day. Participants received Plumpy'Nut, a fortified peanut butter–like paste that contains essential macro- and micronutrients, classified as a RUTF used as an outpatient treatment for SAM. , Plumpy'Nut is manufactured by Nutrik, a subsidiary of the Nutriset Group, based in Kano, Nigeria, the location of our randomized controlled trial. The nutritional objective was to supplement and not replace the calories derived from the habitual daily diet. Children aged from 5.00 to 8.99 years were given 1 daily sachet (500 calories), whereas those aged from 9.00 to 12.99 years received 2 daily (1000 calories) for 12 weeks. Standardization of anthropometric evaluation At each visit, participants underwent a complete anthropometric evaluation with research-quality equipment. Height was measured to the nearest 0.1 cm using a calibrated stadiometer (ShorrBoard Measuring Board, Weigh and Measure, Olney, MD), and weight was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg using a calibrated digital scale (Seca 874 doctor’s scale, Seca, CA). The BMI was calculated by dividing weight (kg) by height squared (m 2 ). Using the World Health Organization’s growth reference, anthropometric measurements were converted to age- and sex-specific z scores. For children aged >10 years, we used Canadian Pediatric Endocrine Group growth charts to calculate weight-for-age z scores. SAM was defined as a BMI z score of <−3.0. All anthropometric measurements were performed in triplicates and averaged to ensure accuracy. If the smallest and largest values had a difference greater than the maximum allowable difference, the measurements were repeated ( ). Before study initiation, the Nigerian team members completed training on proper anthropometric methods, including correct measurement techniques and documentation. To receive anthropometric certification, team members underwent a hands-on assessment, during which they recorded a series of anthropometric measurements of the participants and presented proper techniques and documentation. Research visits After randomization, study participants were closely monitored for 12 weeks. A visit was conducted within 3 or 5 days of starting the RUTF intervention to monitor for electrolyte abnormalities and refeeding syndrome. Every subsequent visit (conducted every 4 weeks) included a comprehensive clinical history, physical examination, anthropometric measurements, and a complete blood count. Between clinic visits, weekly phone calls were made to monitor for interim hospitalizations. As per standard care practices for SAM, all children received antibiotics (amoxicillin) and deworming treatment (albendazole). Children with SCA were prescribed folic acid, antimalarial prophylaxis (Proguanil), and penicillin up to 10 years of age as part of routine care. Parents received face-to-face education on nutrition and hygiene practices throughout the study period. Participants with SCA who experienced weight loss or continued to have a BMI z score of < −3.0 after the 12-week period were eligible for a 12-week trial extension. During this extension period, eligible participants received moderate-dose hydroxyurea and 4or 5 daily RUTF sachets (2000-2500 calories per day). Results from the 12-week extension are part of a separate analysis. Outcomes The protocol-specified primary outcome was to evaluate the feasibility of a malnutrition randomized controlled trial in older children with SCA, via recruitment, retention, and adherence rates during the 12-week intervention period. The recruitment rate was the number of eligible participants who provided informed consent. The retention rate was the proportion of participants who completed the 12-week trial. Adherence to monthly visits was assessed based on the number of missed visits, whereas adherence to the RUTF was evaluated based on the proportion of empty food sachets returned at each visit. The adherence rate for hydroxyurea was determined based on the pill count and an increase in mean corpuscular volume and fetal Hb levels at study exit compared with the levels at baseline. To monitor the safety and AEs during each 4-week visit, we obtained an interval medical history to track any changes in their health status. In addition, a complete blood count

The adherence rate for hydroxyurea was determined based on the pill count and an increase in mean corpuscular volume and fetal Hb levels at study exit compared with the levels at baseline. To monitor the safety and AEs during each 4-week visit, we obtained an interval medical history to track any changes in their health status. In addition, a complete blood count was conducted at baseline and at every 4-week visit to monitor for hydroxyurea toxicity. To monitor for refeeding syndrome, we measured electrolytes twice during the first week: at baseline and 3 or 5 days after initiating the RUTF. We considered any electrolyte derangement during the study as a complication of treatment. As previously done in trials at our laboratory, hospitalizations were adjudicated for the primary reason for admission in the following hierarchal and mutually exclusive categories: stroke, acute chest syndrome, pain, or fever, as detailed in the study protocol ( ). We followed the Common Toxicity Criteria for Adverse Events to evaluate the severity of the AEs. We classified severe AEs (SAEs) as those resulting in prolonged hospitalization (>7 days), admission to the intensive care unit, significant or persistent disability, near death, or death. Randomization and masking To randomize participants, the study statistician constructed allocation tables using a permuted block allocation scheme based on block sizes of 4, stratified based on sex, within the site. The tables were loaded into Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) and used to randomize the participants (1:1) by an unblinded study pharmacist after determining eligibility. The participants went to the trial pharmacists, who distributed the trial medication to their guardians. Allocation was concealed from all other study personnel, except statisticians, because of the requirement to prepare interim reports for the DSMB. Sample size Because our primary goal was to assess the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial of this nature in northern Nigeria, we did not perform sample size calculations. Instead, the final sample size was determined based on budgetary constraints. Statistical analysis Data were collected and managed with REDCap hosted at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. We summarized continuous variables as means and standard deviations (SDs) or as medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) for variables not normally distributed. Categorical variables and prevalence were reported as numbers and percentages. For comparisons between groups, χ 2 test or Fisher exact test was used for percentages, a t test for means, and a Mann-Whitney U test for medians. We used 2 regression models to study the characteristics associated with weight gain for all participants with SCD. Per protocol, we used a logistic regression model to study whether participants achieved a BMI z score of at least −3.0 and whether they achieved at least a 15% weight gain. Finally, because of the evidence that weight-for-age z score is associated with mortality in children with SCA in the same age range living in northern Nigeria, we used the same covariates for the logistic mode for a linear regression model to study the change in weight-for-age z score from baseline. Results Enrollment, randomization, and follow-up In August 2021, the study commenced its screening and enrollment process. At the end of November 2021 (at month 4 of 6), enrollment was paused to prepare for the DSMB meeting held in December. During the pause for the DSMB meeting, the study investigators elected to determine the reason for the low absolute weight gain in the entire cohort. Although the original protocol included a provision for increasing support to families, it was not until December 2021 that this measure was implemented to improve participant outcomes. Specifically, an extra daily sachet could be provided in addition to the existing sachet allocation for participants who were not gaining sufficient weight. Enrollment was restarted in March 2022 and completed in May 2022. A total of 3190 children aged from 5 to 12 years with SCA were evaluated for eligibility during regularly scheduled clinic appointments. Of these children, 4.2% (n = 134) were found to have SAM (BMI z score of <−3.0; ; for specific site enrollment, see ). One eligible child did not enroll in the trial, resulting in an overall enrollment rate of 99.1% (110 of 111). None of the participants in the treatment group withdrew voluntarily from the trial, indicating a retention rate of 100%. One participant died from an unrelated cause (motor vehicle accident). Another participant was enrolled based on the World Health Organization’s table of BMI z scores for sex and age but was administratively withdrawn because of a calculated BMI z score of >−3.0. None of the participants in the treatment group withdrew voluntarily from the trial, indicating a retention rate of 100%. One participant died from an unrelated cause (motor vehicle accident). Another participant was enrolled based on the World Health Organization’s table of BMI z scores for sex and age but was administratively withdrawn because of a calculated BMI z score of >−3.0. This participant completed the 12-week trial but was not included in the analysis. The final analysis included 108 participants, with 54 participants from each arm ( ). If a participant enrolled, siblings aged from 5 to 12 years without SCA were asked to present to the clinic for screening for possible study enrollment. A total of 73 siblings were screened, with 30% classified as having SAM (n = 22) and otherwise eligible for the trial. All eligible siblings elected to enroll (enrollment rate of 100%) and completed the trial (retention rate of 100%). Baseline characteristics Baseline characteristics were balanced across the randomization groups ( ). The median age of participants in the RUTF-only and RUTF-plus-hydroxyurea groups was 10.5 and 10.2 years, respectively ( P = .232; ), and the baseline BMI z scores for the RUTF-only and RUTF-plus-hydroxyurea arms were not statistically different (−3.66 vs −3.64; P = .821). No significant differences were found between the baseline demographics and clinical parameters of those randomly assigned to RUTF only or RUTF plus hydroxyurea ( ). Adherence Per protocol, all participants were expected to attend research visits every 4 weeks for interval history, physical examination, anthropometric measurements, and laboratory surveillance. None of the scheduled visits were missed. The median percentage of RUTF sachets returned empty was 100% (IQR, 99.98-100). After the DSMB meeting in December 2022, questions on food sharing were added to the study because the aggregated group results indicated that many participants had a BMI z score of <−3.0 at the study end point and indirect evidence from interviews that the participants were sharing the RUTF. Of the 70 participants with available data on sharing, the majority (62.9%; n = 44) reported at least sometimes sharing the RUTF ( ). Multiple hydroxyurea adherence measurements were performed. The median percentage of pills returned was 4.4% (IQR, 0.00-8.27; n = 54). The mean increase in mean corpuscular volume was higher in the group receiving RUTF plus hydroxyurea than in that with only RUTF (5.4 vs −1.0; P = .007; ). The median HbF level increased by 2.2% (IQR, 0.5-4.9) and 3.9% (IQR, 1.7-6.8) from baseline to study exit in the RUTF-only and RUTF-plus-hydroxyurea groups, respectively ( ). Additional laboratory values demonstrating the anticipated hydroxyurea response from baseline to study exit are shown in . Safety During the 12-week trial, there were 4 hospitalizations in the RUTF-only group and 2 hospitalizations in the RUTF-plus-hydroxyurea group ( P = .678). Hospitalization diagnoses included pain (2 hospitalizations), acute chest syndrome, fever, and other (elective surgery for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy; anemia with an inadequate investigation to determine etiology, splenic sequestration, parvovirus B19, or malaria). One hospitalization was prolonged and met the criteria for an SAE but was deemed unrelated to the study treatment. One participant died from a motor vehicle accident unrelated to the study treatment before completing the trial. No participant had hydroxyurea discontinued due to myelosuppression or drug-related toxicity, and no participant required dose reductions. The baseline and study-exit hematology laboratory values per treatment group are displayed in . Electrolytes were evaluated at baseline in 100% of participants (110 of 110) and repeated 3 or 5 days after starting RUTF in 98% of the participants (108 of 110 participants; ). No participant developed hypophosphatemia ( ). There were no clinical cases of refeeding syndrome. Efficacy results The mean baseline BMI z score was −3.7 (SD = 0.5) and increased to −3.2 (SD = 0.5) at the study end point, for a change of 0.49 (SD = 0.53; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.39-0.59; n = 108; ), and 61.1% of participants continued to have SAM ( ). Factors postulated to be associated with treatment response were analyzed in a multivariable linear regression model. A higher baseline BMI z score predicted a higher end point BMI z score (β = 0.64; P ≤ .001; ), whereas older age predicted a lower BMI z score at 12 weeks (β = −0.06; P ≤ .023; ). The treatment group was not significantly associated with the BMI z score at 12 weeks (β = 0.01; P = .928). We, then, constructed a multivariable logistic regression with the same covariates to assess covariates associated with continued SAM (BMI z score of <−3.0) after 12 weeks (treatment nonresponse). A higher baseline BMI z score predicted a higher end point BMI z score (β = 0.64; P ≤ .001; ), whereas older age predicted a lower BMI z score at 12 weeks (β = −0.06; P ≤ .023; ). The treatment group was not significantly associated with the BMI z score at 12 weeks (β = 0.01; P = .928). We, then, constructed a multivariable logistic regression with the same covariates to assess covariates associated with continued SAM (BMI z score of <−3.0) after 12 weeks (treatment nonresponse). Baseline BMI z score and age remained significant in the logistic model to predict continued SAM ( ). Among all participants, for every additional year of age, the odds of remaining severely malnourished increased (odds ratio [OR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.01-1.57; P = .041; ; A). Increasing baseline BMI z score level up to <−3.0 was associated with decreased odds of remaining severely malnourished (OR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.05-0.47; P = .001; ; B). For participants who did and who did not achieve a study-exit BMI z score ≥ −3.0, the change in BMI z score was greater for children with lower baseline BMI z scores ( ). No participant with a baseline BMI z score <−4.4 improved their BMI to ≥−3.0 during the study. Weight gain of at least 15% was uncommon; only 9.3% (10 of 110) had a 15% weight gain. Given the low percentage of participants with 15% weight gain, a limited model demonstrated that participants with higher baseline BMI z score were less likely to increase weight by 15% (OR, 0.19; 95% CI, 0.04-0.88; P = .034; ). Participants in the RUTF-plus-hydroxyurea group had 4.6 higher odds of achieving a 15% weight gain but did not reach statistical significance (95% CI, 0.99-21.3; P = .052). The mean change in weight-for-age z score was 0.28 (SD = 0.298). Male sex and older age predicted a lower weight-for-age z score at 12 weeks (sex: β = −0.12; P = .039; age β = −0.03; P = .044; ). Discussion Malnutrition and SCD are common comorbidities in sub-Saharan Africa. , However, no evidence-based guidelines have developed the optimal management when both comorbidities occur simultaneously. To our knowledge, the SAMS trial is the first randomized controlled trial to demonstrate the feasibility and safety of outpatient treatment of severely malnourished children aged from 5 to 12 years with SCA. An accurate diagnosis of SAM was made in 99% of children (109 of 110), with no participant defaulting on treatment and no SAEs associated with malnutrition treatment. Weight and BMI increased during the 12-week intervention with supplemental RUTF, with or without hydroxyurea. A significant public health finding was the lower rate of SAMS in our malnutrition trial (4.2%) than in our primary stroke prevention trial (20.9%) in the same region. Most likely, this discrepancy was due to the enhanced fidelity of anthropometric assessment after rigorous training and measurement protocols for the research in the malnutrition trial. However, the SAM prevalence in children aged >5 years with SCA in this study is higher than in children aged <5 years in the same region (Kano, Nigeria; 1.5%; n = 754), emphasizing that SAM remains a public health concern in older children with SCA. All the feasibility and safety measures were met during the 12-week intervention period. Notably, we had no missed visits; the acceptable default rate (≥2 missed weighing visits) is 15% for children aged <5 years, as set by the Sphere Association’s Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response, with default rates in the practice ranging from 5% to 40%. Furthermore, the data suggest that hydroxyurea therapy is safe for severely malnourished children, a population previously excluded from an important study on the safety of hydroxyurea therapy in sub-Saharan Africa but not excluded from other clinical trials with hydroxyurea. , , , Based on our data, and data from other studies, we believe the risk-benefit ratio should not exclude children with SAM from hydroxyurea treatment unless definitive evidence indicates direct harm to the child. An unexpected important finding was that >50% of the children shared their RUTF. The adherence rates to the RUTF were overall very high, as was the rate of sharing, which may explain the variability in response to treatment. Sharing supplements with other household members has been reported in other studies and highlights cultural imperatives and moral obligations to feed all family members, which can hinder the strategy of deliberative targeting of food supplements. , In children with HIV aged from 5 to 18 years, 38% of caregivers and participants reported sharing ready-to-use food (RUF), with caregivers reporting that they felt other adults or children needed the RUF. In a study for outpatient treatment of severe and moderate malnutrition in

were overall very high, as was the rate of sharing, which may explain the variability in response to treatment. Sharing supplements with other household members has been reported in other studies and highlights cultural imperatives and moral obligations to feed all family members, which can hinder the strategy of deliberative targeting of food supplements. , In children with HIV aged from 5 to 18 years, 38% of caregivers and participants reported sharing ready-to-use food (RUF), with caregivers reporting that they felt other adults or children needed the RUF. In a study for outpatient treatment of severe and moderate malnutrition in children with HIV, 32% of caregivers admitted to consuming the RUF themselves. Strategies to reduce sharing, such as the rationalization of RUF prescription, the enrollment of other undernourished family members in RUF therapy, and food complements for the household, have not been systematically evaluated. , As a secondary outcome, we assessed the anthropometric measures. Our main conclusion from the anthropometric measures during the 12 weeks of the trial was that providing 500 or 1000 additional calories may not be sufficient for SAM recovery, particularly in those in food sharing settings and with very low baseline BMI z scores. A study of older children with HIV and a median age of 11 years treated for moderate or SAM in Ethiopia reported that only 65% recovered from malnutrition during a 6-month period. Possible reasons for the lower magnitude of our treatment response could be attributable to the use of only supplemental calories from RUTF, the common practice of food sharing, and the length of the intervention. As a feasibility study, the sample size was not based on determining the difference in efficacy of the 2 treatment arms. We could not analyze daily calories and nutrient intake from the habitual diet because of limited food composition databases and difficulty quantifying the amount of food consumed as part of shared meals. A limitation of the malnutrition trial was its failure to assess pubertal status, which could have influenced the study outcomes; however, there was not a significant change in absolute height for females during the trial, indicating the pubertal growth spurt was an unlikely confounder for our trial. These limitations do not affect the primary trial outcome measures, demonstrating the feasibility of our treatment strategy. The results will guide future definitive trials on treating SAM in older children with SCA. In the first NIH-funded malnutrition trial for SCA, outpatient treatment of SAM with RUTF and hydroxyurea was safe and feasible for children aged from 5 to 12 years in a low-income setting. This trial supports the safety of hydroxyurea therapy in low-income settings, even with concomitant SAM. The results indicate promise for the effects of RUTF and hydroxyurea on improved nutritional status. Future studies should consider more intensive interventions (ie, higher target daily calories from RUTF), with longer durations and the inclusion of the cultural aspect of food sharing in the trial design. Our team is planning a larger scale randomized controlled phase 3 trial to evaluate the effectiveness of hydroxyurea and RUTF for SAM treatment in children aged from 5 to 12 years in northern Nigeria. documents.title: ASH 2020 Guidelines for Sickle Cell Disease Cerebrovascular Disease Prevention

chunks.content: Introduction Sickle cell disease is the most common abnormality detected on newborn screening, affecting 1 in 375 African-American subjects and almost 90 000 individuals overall in the United States. The more severe forms of sickle cell disease (hemoglobin SS, hemoglobin Sβ 0 thalassemia), referred to as sickle cell anemia, occur in 1 in 400 African-American newborns. Sickle cell anemia–related neurologic morbidity from cerebrovascular complications can be severe. The most common cause of permanent neurologic injury in children and adults with sickle cell anemia is a silent cerebral infarct, occurring in ∼39% of children by age 18 years. Silent cerebral infarcts require magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to detect and a formal neurologic examination to exclude the presence of an overt stroke. Silent cerebral infarcts are progressive in both children and adults. Silent cerebral infarcts are associated with at least a 5-point full-scale intelligence quotient drop in children, and with biologically plausible evidence to indicate a similar degree of neurologic morbidity in adults. Once silent cerebral infarcts are identified, children and adults are eligible for evaluation for Individualized Education Plans and Americans with Disability Act services, respectively. Most silent cerebral infarcts occur in the brain’s border zone regions, including the frontal lobe, which disproportionately affect executive function. The American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine has formally endorsed evidence-based strategies to support individuals with executive dysfunction. In 2020, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) published evidence-based guidelines for preventing, diagnosing, and treating cerebrovascular disease in children and adults with sickle cell disease. The guideline panel developed clinical recommendations and assessed the certainty of the supporting evidence based on evidence-to-decision factors using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations approach. The evidence-to-decision factors, which determined the clinical guideline recommendations, ask for an assessment of the effects of interventions and resource utilization (cost-effectiveness), among others. Although the effects of stroke prevention interventions were based on 5 completed National Institutes of Health–sponsored randomized controlled trials, no assessment of resource utilization has been performed in the SIT (Silent Cerebral Infarct Transfusion) Trial to accompany the benefits of regular blood transfusions to prevent cerebral infarct recurrence. This lack of cost-effectiveness evaluation is a gap in the current ASH guidelines for treating children with preexisting silent cerebral infarcts. To fill this gap in informed decision-making regarding the treatment of silent cerebral infarcts with regular blood transfusion therapy, we conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of blood transfusion therapy to prevent cerebral infarct recurrence in children with preexisting silent cerebral infarcts participating in the SIT Trial. Regular blood transfusion therapy significantly reduced recurrent cerebral infarcts in children with sickle cell anemia in the SIT Trial. Regular blood transfusion therapy is costly, burdensome, and associated with an increased iron burden and iron overload–associated morbidity. Furthermore, the impact of lowering the incidence of silent and overt strokes in sickle cell anemia on costs related to other aspects of the lives of individuals with sickle cell (eg, education) remained unanswered. We performed a cost-effectiveness analysis to address a critical gap in understanding the tradeoffs between monthly blood transfusions vs standard care to prevent infarct recurrence (silent or overt stroke) in children with preexisting silent cerebral infarcts. We included the costs associated with medical care (hospitalization, emergency department visit, transfusion, and outpatient care) and indirect costs of special education. Materials and methods Parent study The current analyses were conducted as a secondary aim of the SIT Trial. The trial’s primary aim was to determine whether regular blood transfusion therapy reduced overt stroke incidence and new or worsening silent cerebral infarcts among children with sickle cell anemia and a history of silent cerebral infarcts. Children aged 5 to 15 years with sickle cell anemia (defined as hemoglobin SS or hemoglobin Sβ 0 thalassemia) were enrolled from 3 December 2004, to 3 December 2010, with all follow-up completed as of 29 July 2013. After a screening MRI to exclude children without prior silent cerebral infarct, study candidates underwent transcranial Doppler screening. Children whose transcranial Doppler result was above the transfusion threshold (nonimaging method, ≥200 cm/sec; imaging method, ≥185 cm/sec) were excluded. Eligible children underwent a full MRI protocol immediately before randomization, including optional magnetic resonance angiography. We recorded the primary reason for hospitalization and the length of stay for each participant during the trial. The institutional review board approved the SIT Trial at each participating institution. The SIT Trial is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov (# NCT00072761 ). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Intervention In the original trial, 196 children were randomly assigned to receive standard care (herein referred to as the standard care group) or regular blood transfusions (herein referred to as the transfusion group) for at least 36 months or until a study end point was reached. Participants who were randomly assigned to the standard care group received no treatment of silent

for each participant during the trial. The institutional review board approved the SIT Trial at each participating institution. The SIT Trial is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov (# NCT00072761 ). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Intervention In the original trial, 196 children were randomly assigned to receive standard care (herein referred to as the standard care group) or regular blood transfusions (herein referred to as the transfusion group) for at least 36 months or until a study end point was reached. Participants who were randomly assigned to the standard care group received no treatment of silent infarcts, including no hydroxyurea therapy. They were seen biannually as outpatients with complete blood count laboratory testing. Participants in the transfusion group received either automated exchange transfusion (recommended) or simple or partial exchange transfusion (acceptable), initially at 2-week intervals until the hemoglobin S levels were reduced to 30% or lower and at 4-week intervals after that. Participants in the transfusion group also received regular iron chelation therapy to reduce complications associated with transfusion-related iron overload. For the current study, the transfusion group was determined by using a protocol approach, with all participants included who received regular transfusions over at least 6 months, irrespective of the original group assignment. Descriptive analyses were performed for demographic characteristics and clinical features of participants in the SIT Trial. Means and standard deviations are reported for continuous variables, and proportions are reported for categorical variables. Various statistical tests, including the Mann-Whitney U test, χ 2 test, mid- P exact test, and permutation test, were performed to compare those variables between the standard care and transfusion groups. Statistical analyses were conducted by using SPSS version 26 (IBM SPSS Statistics, IBM Corporation), and statistical significance was set at P < .05. Outcomes and measures The primary sickle cell anemia–related outcomes were hospitalizations at participating hospitals. Data for hospitalizations occurring at non-study hospitals were not available and thus were not considered. Based on primary discharge diagnosis, hospitalizations were categorized primarily due to the following order’s hierarchical categories: acute chest syndrome (ACS), pain, fever or infection, exchange transfusion, surgery, or asthma. Follow-up occurred from random allocation to primary end point (an overt stroke or new or progression of silent cerebral infarct) or exit MRI, whichever came first. Cost data Direct medical costs. Direct medical costs included hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and outpatient costs. Hospitalizations. The Children Hospital Association’s Pediatric Health Information System (PHIS) database was used to estimate costs per day of hospitalization. Currently, the PHIS database includes clinical and billing data from 49 tertiary care children’s hospitals located in noncompeting markets of 27 states plus Washington, DC, accounting for ∼20% of annual pediatric hospitalizations in the United States. De-identified data submitted by participating hospitals include an encrypted medical record number, which allows tracking of individuals to the same hospital over time. In addition, data quality is ensured through a joint effort between the Children’s Hospital Association and participating hospitals. Between 2003 and 2010, PHIS membership increased from 35 to 45 hospitals, with 14 US SIT Trial institutions (48% of the 29 SIT Trial institutions) contributing to PHIS cost estimates. Total costs for each hospitalization were calculated by PHIS adjusted with each hospital’s annual costs-to-charges ratio for each year, using the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wage/price index for the given hospital’s location. Inpatient costs were based on length of hospital stay, modified by the occurrence of categories of adverse events in the following non-overlapping hierarchy: ACS: admissions with International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) code 517.3, without any codes for stroke. Vaso-occlusive pain episodes (including avascular necrosis, headache, priapism, and acute anemia): admissions with ICD-9-CM code 282.xx, without ACS and stroke codes, and generic drug codes for opiates. Fever/infection: admission with any SS disorder code without ACS and stroke codes and with 1 of 1500 ICD-9-CM infectious disease codes. Exchange transfusion: admission with an ICD-9-CM code for sickle cell disorders plus procedure code for exchange transfusion. Surgery: admission with an ICD-9-CM code for sickle cell disorders without ACS and stroke codes and a surgical All Patients Refined Diagnosis Related Groups code. Asthma: admission with any sickle cell SS disorder code and asthma code (493.xx) without ACS and stroke codes or generic drug codes for opiates. Our goal was to estimate the costs of hospitalizations for most participants in our cost analyses for sickle cell complications. Although the length of stay was not normally distributed, we used an established statistical calculation to exclude high outliers using a cutoff of the 75th percentile (Q3) plus 1.5 times the interquartile range of the length of stay for a given participant subset. This method resulted in an overall mean length of stay cutoff of 9.5 days, with a range of 8.5 days for hospitalizations for suspected infection with

without ACS and stroke codes or generic drug codes for opiates. Our goal was to estimate the costs of hospitalizations for most participants in our cost analyses for sickle cell complications. Although the length of stay was not normally distributed, we used an established statistical calculation to exclude high outliers using a cutoff of the 75th percentile (Q3) plus 1.5 times the interquartile range of the length of stay for a given participant subset. This method resulted in an overall mean length of stay cutoff of 9.5 days, with a range of 8.5 days for hospitalizations for suspected infection with a fever to 12 days for ACS. Linear regression modeling was then performed on the total cost per hospitalization vs length of stay graph to develop a cost per day for each adverse event type. Inpatient costs were projected to be 54.3% lower ($4929 vs $10 802 per year) for the transfusion and standard care groups, respectively, correlating with the reduction in annual length of stay. Reported estimates for professional fees ranged between 17.7% and 26.4% of facility costs of hospitalization. Emergency department visits. Costs for emergency department visits for vaso-occlusive pain episodes and ACS were developed by using a similar clinical algorithm for hospitalizations. The 14 PHIS hospitals represented in the SIT Trial were queried for emergency department encounters for vaso-occlusive pain episodes and ACS in 2020. The mean and standard deviation cost for each encounter type were calculated. Outpatient services. We included outpatient medical expenses from the PHIS and available literature for transfusion, including physician costs, laboratory tests, surveillance, and expenses for blood transfusions. Physician cost for an outpatient visit was estimated based on work relative value units for a Current Procedural Terminology code of 99215 (2.80) and compensation per work relative value units ($36.09). A laboratory test for a complete blood count was $7 from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services clinical laboratory fee schedule. An annual liver iron content scan was between $400 reported by Wood et al to $5865 based on costs from a PHIS site. Costs of blood transfusions were estimated from several sources. Costs for blood transfusion estimates ranged from $616 to $1706 for transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells by simple transfusion or partial exchange. Costs for therapeutic erythrocytapheresis (herein referred to as apheresis) were obtained from a participating SIT center. Apheresis costs were $3452 per procedure and $44 871 annually. Iron chelation costs were based on a child who weighed 29 kg (median weight among participants in the SIT Trial) and received deferasirox, an oral iron chelator, at the standard dose of 20 mg/kg per day. We used deferasirox for our base case because this iron chelation agent is the first-line assessment for iron chelation therapy for regular transfusion therapy in sickle cell anemia. Given the typical tablet size for deferasirox (500 mg), we used this for the daily dose estimate for the mean study participant for oral iron chelation. Costs for a 500-mg tablet of generic deferasirox ranged from $112 to $192 as obtained from Lexicomp. The mean of the low and high end of the range ($152 per tablet) was used for the base case, yielding a yearly cost of $55 440. We also obtained deferoxamine cost as an alternative or additional iron chelation therapy. A 500-mg vial of deferoxamine cost was obtained from the pharmacy at participating SIT centers ($13.45). Costs of home administration of subcutaneous deferoxamine were $28 per day as estimated in consultation with a home infusion company serving a participating center. Based on these estimates, the cost of deferoxamine was $11 008 per year. Indirect costs of special education. Using data from the academic year of 1999 to 2000, and adjusting for inflation, other education expenditures for a student with a cerebral infarct range from $16 359 to $31 134 per year depending on the degree of their disabilities (mean for our base case, $23 746 per year). For these differences in education costs, the potential savings would be $14 384 per year for every cerebral infarct prevented. In the SIT Trial, 6 (6%) participants in the transfusion group had cerebral infarct recurrence, and 16 (14%) had infarct recurrence in the standard care group. Therefore, the annual cost of special education would be $7402 for the transfusion group and $8280 for the standard care group, yielding a savings of $2634 over the 3-year time horizon.
