Recent data from the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic suggested that greater psychological flexibility was robustly associated with lower mental health symptoms, including depressive, anxious, and stress symptoms. Despite broader interest in these constructs and their potential overlap, very few studies have attempted to delineate how different coping styles, psychological flexibility dimensions, and other related psychological constructs are associated with mental health outcomes. The objective of the present study was to characterize the associations between psychological flexibility, coping styles, and tendencies towards over-vs-under controlled behaviors with negative affect, as well as the relative magnitude of association between these various coping-related constructs. The present study attempted to characterize these associations in a large sample of adult PwCF, for whom coping with their chronic condition is an important and under-studied determinant of quality of life and clinical outcomes. METHODS Participants The present cohort was comprised of 124 PwCF (87 females, 37 males) from baseline assessments of a randomized, telehealth ACT trial ( https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04114227 ; NCT04114227 ). The parent trial included 124 adult PwCF, all of whom were utilized in the present analyses. The parent trial recruited individuals from four primary sites (Thomas Jefferson University, University of Virginia, Duke University Medical Center, Augusta University) who were then randomized to receive six sessions of either ACT or supportive (non-directed) psychotherapy over the course of six weeks. As shown in , participants tended to be White, had previously participated in psychotherapy, were taking psychotropic medications at the time of participation, and exhibited elevated anxiety and/or depressive symptoms. Inclusion criteria were age of 18 or older, diagnosis of CF, and a score of 4 or higher on the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and/or the Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Consent was obtained electronically or in person. Sessions were conducted through telehealth using a Health Insurance Portability Accountability Act-compliant Zoom webcam platform. The Thomas Jefferson University IRB was the IRB of record, and participating sites also obtained IRB approval from their institutions. Measures The present cross-sectional analyses are based on baseline data from a previously reported randomized ACT trial among PwCF. Participants completed a demographic questionnaire and psychometric measures of depression [Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II)], anxiety [Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI)], cognitive fusion [Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire (CFQ)-13, Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ)-II], quality of life [Cystic Fibrosis Mental Health and Wellness Questionnaire; Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R)], treatment adherence (Treatment Adherence Questionnaire-CF), and coping (Medical Coping Modes Questionnaire, Coping Flexibility Scale, Short Grit Scale, Styles of Coping Word-Pairs) at baseline, posttreatment, and 3-month follow-up. Negative Affect To examine associations between coping, psychological flexibility, and control styles with mood-related variables, we utilized two canonical measures of depressive and anxious symptoms, which were combined for analysis (see “ ” section). We elected not to use the screening measures above (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9) in either the primary trial or the present analyses, as we wanted to minimize bias associated with annual, repeated administrations of these routinely obtained screening measures. The Beck Depression Inventory-II The BDI-II is a 21-item self-report measuring symptoms of depression over the past two weeks. Item responses range from 0 to 3, and total scores from 0 to 63, with higher scores indicating higher levels of symptoms. Total BDI-II scores are conventionally interpreted as 0 to 13 suggesting minimal depressive symptoms, 14 to 19 suggesting mild symptoms, 20 to 28 suggesting moderate symptoms, and 29 to 63 suggesting severe depressive symptoms. The Beck Anxiety Inventory The BAI is a 21-item self-report measure assessing symptoms of anxiety over the past week. Answer options range from 0 (not at all) to 3 (severely), and total scores range from 0 to 63, with higher scores indicating higher levels of anxiety symptoms. Total BAI scores are conventionally interpreted as 0 to 7 suggesting minimal anxiety symptoms, 8 to 15 suggesting mild symptoms, 16 to 25 suggesting moderate symptoms, and 26 to 63 suggesting severely elevated anxiety symptoms. We selected the 2 measures below because they are the most widely used within the ACT literature and associated with the 2 subdomains most strongly associated with symptomatic improvements from psychological interventions. Psychological Flexibility To assess psychological flexibility, we collected data using two of the most commonly deployed measures assessing subcomponents of psychological flexibility and the degree to which individuals reported engagement with values-consistent behaviors in their daily lives. We selected the 2 measures below because they are the most widely used within the ACT literature and associated with the 2 subdomains most strongly associated with symptomatic improvements from psychological interventions. These 2 canonical variables were combined to provide a mean rank score of psychological flexibility (see “ ” section). The Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire-13 The CFQ-13 is a 13-item self-report measure of cognitive fusion, which is best understood as the degree of rigid attachment one has to their thought content and the tendency for thoughts to dictate behaviors. For example, individuals who tend to overthink their responses, become “stuck in their head,” and who may actively try to keep themselves from having unwanted thoughts (which they cannot fully control) would be considered to have more cognitive fusion. Responses range from 1 (not true at all) to 7 (always true), and total scores from 13 to 91, with higher scores indicating a greater degree of cognitive fusion. The Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II The AAQ-II is a 7-item measure of psychological flexibility. Responses range from 1 (never true) to 7 (always true), and higher scores indicate higher levels of inflexibility/experiential avoidance. Medical Coping Modes Questionnaire The Medical Coping Modes Questionnaire is a 20-item self-report measure for use with patients with a life-threatening disease. Domains of confrontation, avoidance, and resignation are measured. Items are rated from 0 (never) to 4 (always), and the domain with the highest score reflects the coping style most likely to be used. Coping Flexibility Scale The Coping Flexibility Scale is a 10-item measure of coping flexibility, with subscales of evaluation of coping (ineffective) and adaptive coping. Respondents rate how stress-coping situations relate to them on a scale from 1 (not true) to 4 (very true). Total scores range from 10 to 40, with higher scores indicating more flexible coping styles. The Short Grit Scale The Short Grit Scale is a self-report measure of “grit,” or trait-level perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Respondents rate how well statements described them on a 5-point scale, from “not like me at all” to “very much like me.” Total scores are averaged across all items and, therefore, range from 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating greater levels of self-reported grit. The Styles of Coping Word-Pairs Questionnaire The Styles of Coping Word-Pairs , is a 47-item forced-choice measure of overall personality style. Scores indicate if the respondent’s coping style tends to be more over-controlled or undercontrolled. Higher scores indicate greater tendencies towards response patterns characterized by exerting greater levels of control. Participant Health Information Data regarding lung function were extracted from participants’ electronic health records and included forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC; the total amount of air that can be exhaled), and FEV 1 /FVC ratio. Data Analyses Analyses were conducted in SAS 9.4 and R 4.4.3. Sample size was determined at the time of the initial grant application for the parent trial. General linear models were used to examine the associations between coping styles and psychological outcomes, controlling for age, sex, and pulmonary function. To reduce the total number of analyses and mitigate against type-I error, psychological outcomes were combined into a mean rank, global score. , We have used this approach extensively to enhance power in small sample sizes and reduce multiplicity among highly interrelated outcome measures, both of which are common within behavioral trials utilizing psychometric outcomes. – We elected to combine our two measures of psychological flexibility (CFQ-13 and the AAQ-II) based both on their shared conceptual overlap and their high degree of intercorrelation in the present sample (r = 0.75, p < .001). We also conducted secondary analyses to characterize levels of depressive and anxious symptoms among individuals with high (ie, the top quartile) versus low (ie, the lowest quartile) psychological flexibility. Similarly, the negative effect was comprised of the BDI-II and BAI. Sample size estimates for the parent trial were based on conservative assumptions from prior behavioral intervention trials, which assumed an r-squared between covariates and the outcome of interest of 0.50, a 30% attrition rate, and an approximate effect size of Cohen d = 0.45. Multiple imputation using PROC MI in SAS 9.4 with 200 imputations was used to account for missing data (<5%). Data and/or code for all analyses are available upon request from the corresponding author. Among the 124 individuals who were available at baseline and provided psychometric data, 74 (60%) were taking psychotropic medication. FEV 1 /FVC ratios varied widely [median = 76% (interquartile range = 66, 85)], and participants demonstrated a strong tendency towards over-vs-under control [median log-transformed control style = 5.4 (5.0, 5.8)]. Depressive [BDI-II = 18.6 (SD = 9.9)] and anxious [BAI = 13.8 (SD = 9.3)] symptoms were both elevated. Fifty participants (39%) were married, and most participants were using modulator therapy at the time of randomization. Acceptance and Action scores and Cognitive Fusion scores were highly correlated and, therefore, combined into a mean rank and global score to assess their association with mood (mean rank combination of the BDI-II and BAI). Psychological Flexibility, Coping, and Mood displays unadjusted correlations between different coping measures, psychological flexibility, and behavioral control styles. Greater levels of psychological flexibility were associated with lower negative affect (B = −0.60, p < .001, , ). Follow-up analyses revealed robust associations between negative affect and both acceptance (B = −0.51. p < .001, ) and cognitive fusion (B = −0.59, p < .001, ). Similarly, greater levels of avoidance (B = 0.32, p < .001), resignation (B = 0.37, p < .001), lower levels of grit (B = −0.35, p < .001), and lower tendencies towards over-vs-under control (B = −0.29, p = .003) all associated with greater negative affect. Additional analyses of baseline data revealed that greater negative affect was associated with worse FEV 1 levels (B = −0.19, p = .046), with the strongest association for the BDI-II (B = −0.22, p = .029). Although our composite measure of psychological flexibility was not associated with FEV 1 levels (B = 0.13, p = .152), exploratory analyses revealed that higher scores on the AAQ-II tended to be associated with FEV 1 (B = 0.17, p = .062). Hierarchical regression analyses demonstrated that greater psychological flexibility was the most robust correlate of lower negative affect after accounting for other coping variables (B = −0.50, p < .001), and this association was not moderated by FEV 1 /FVC levels. Explanatory analyses revealed that lower levels of cognitive fusion on the CFQ (B = −0.54, p < .001) and lower psychological acceptance and action on the AAQ-II (B = 0.61, p < .001) were strongly associated with higher levels of negative affect. To characterize clinically meaningful levels of depressive and anxious symptoms, we conducted secondary analyses in which we examined BDI-II and BAI levels among individuals in the lowest quartile of psychological flexibility (ie, ≤25th percentile) compared with individuals in the top quartile (ie, ≥75th percentile). Results suggested that individuals with low compared with high psychological flexibility had clinically meaningful differences in depressive and anxious symptoms. For the BDI-II, individuals with high versus low psychological flexibility had depressive symptom scores corresponding to minimal-mild depressive symptoms versus moderate-severe symptoms [lowest quartile: mean BDI-II = 11.3 (SD = 6.3) vs highest quartile: mean BDI-II = 27.3 (SD = 10.4)]. For anxiety symptoms, high versus low psychological flexibility corresponded to low versus moderate levels of anxiety [lowest quartile: mean BAI = 9.9 (SD = 7.9) vs highest quartile: mean BAI = 22.3 (SD = 9.7)]. To visually display levels of psychological flexibility across levels of depressive symptoms, shows both unadjusted ( ) and adjusted ( ) psychological flexibility scores across levels of depressive symptoms. As shown, greater depressive symptoms are associated with higher (worse) psychological flexibility scores ( p < .001). Within the present sample of PwCF, we demonstrated that multiple measures associated with coping, coping flexibility, grit, and control tendencies are all associated with levels of depression and anxiety. However, markers of psychological flexibility were not only associated more robustly with measures of mood but also remained significantly associated even after controlling for all other measures of coping-related constructs. Within the present sample of PwCF, we demonstrated that multiple measures associated with coping, coping flexibility, grit, and control tendencies are all associated with levels of depression and anxiety. However, markers of psychological flexibility were not only associated more robustly with measures of mood but also remained significantly associated even after controlling for all other measures of coping-related constructs. This finding underscores the potential unique addition that psychological flexibility may provide to enhance understanding of effective coping strategies. These findings are particularly important for PwCF, for whom the past decade has introduced novel therapies (eg, cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator modulators) that have dramatically altered expectations regarding survival and quality of life. , The importance of coping on mood within chronic disease samples has been an area of extensive study over the past several decades. – Prior work has suggested that different coping styles, such as approach-oriented or avoidant coping, may provide critical data to inform targeted treatments to enhance coping abilities. – Notwithstanding the clear importance of proactive coping styles, , data over the past decade have begun to enhance this perspective by underscoring the importance of contextual demands in understanding the relationship between coping and mood. For example, for individuals with a chronic health problem that is unrelenting or less pliable by approach oriented coping styles, efforts to change behavior may not only be ill advised but may also worsen mood and clinically relevant outcomes. , Acceptance-based psychological approaches embrace this important distinction by focusing on the importance of psychological flexibility as an important target to cultivate adaptive coping styles, which may involve some combination of approach, acceptance, or even avoidance of stressors depending on individual contextual challenges. Psychological flexibility has several important components that all contribute to more adaptive coping. These include greater experiential acceptance, lower cognitive fusion, clarity of personal values, self-as-context (ie, having a more stable sense of self that does not change across settings), present moment awareness, and committed action. , Two of the key components that appear most modifiable by treatment within the ACT framework are training individuals to have greater levels of psychological acceptance of uncomfortable experiences in the service of valued actions and greater detachment from their thought content as literally true. Within the present study, both of these constructs are associated robustly with levels of depression and anxiety and thus could be targets of psychological intervention. While there are some elements of psychological flexibility that may be associated with grit, coping styles, and control tendencies, it is possible that acceptance and cognitive fusion may reflect more thought-based aspects of the coping process that are then reflected by a variety of different, more effective behaviors. , The present analyses must be viewed with several important limitations in mind. First, our assessments of coping and other relevant behaviors were obtained almost exclusively from self-report and should, therefore, be interpreted with some caution. Future studies might benefit from additional assessment of behavioral adherents, physical activity, and other clinically relevant health behaviors that are germane to the population of the study. Second, it is unclear to what extent the present findings are unique to individuals with CF or may extend beyond this population. PwCF has unique and chronic health challenges that may require different coping styles for affected behavioral management. It is notable, for example, that individuals in the present sample reported a very high level of over versus undercontrol tendencies, suggesting a high level of engagement and an impulse towards more regimented behavioral responses, which may not generalize to people living with CF as a whole or to other medical populations. Third, our analysis was cross-sectional, and it is unclear to what extent the observed pattern of findings holds across time. Notably, within the present sample, parallel analyses of psychological flexibility and negative affect following 6-weeks of ACT treatment not only replicated findings at baseline but demonstrated stronger associations with flexibility and mood (B = −0.69, p < .001), suggesting that this association may be robust. Future studies should nevertheless replicate the present pattern of associations to ensure their validity. Finally, it should be noted that our sample was likely highly selective in several ways, including socioeconomic status, degree of prior psychotherapy, and degree of psychotropic medication usage. It is, therefore, likely that those individuals who enrolled had higher socioeconomic status and were more inclined to utilize psychological services relative to participants who did not enroll. This may limit the generalizability of these findings to other more representative samples. CONCLUSION Our data underscore the burgeoning body of evidence suggesting that psychological flexibility is an important correlate of mood within PwCF. Moreover, it is possible that psychological flexibility provides a unique and previously underexamined component of coping processes that may enhance our understanding of psychological resilience among individuals with chronic health conditions. Objective: These guidelines of the American Society of Hematology (ASH), based on the best available evidence, are intended to support patients, clinicians, and other health care professionals in their decisions about management of pediatric VTE. Methods: ASH formed a multidisciplinary guideline panel that included 2 patient representatives and was balanced to minimize potential bias from conflicts of interest. The McMaster University GRADE Centre supported the guideline-development process, including updating or performing systematic evidence reviews (up to April of 2017). The panel prioritized clinical questions and outcomes according to their importance for clinicians and patients. The panel used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, including GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks, to assess evidence and make recommendations, which were subject to public comment. Results: The panel agreed on 30 recommendations, covering symptomatic and asymptomatic deep vein thrombosis, with specific focus on management of central venous access device–associated VTE. chunks.content: Introduction: multiple myeloma definition Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy characterized by overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulins (M-proteins) [ ]. This expansion is accompanied by suppression of normal immunoglobulin synthesis and progressive marrow infiltration, which underlies disease pathophysiology. MM represents the second most common hematological malignancy and accounts for 15% of newly diagnosed hematologic cancers and nearly 20% of related mortality. Incidence in Western populations is 5–7 cases per 100,000 persons per year, with a median diagnostic age near 70 years, underscoring its strong age association [ ]. Incidence rises steeply with age [ ]. Clinically, MM is defined by bone marrow infiltration and end-organ damage. Key features include clonal plasma cell proliferation, monoclonal protein production, and organ dysfunction, most frequently involving bone, hematopoiesis, and renal function. Typical manifestations include osteolytic lesions, anemia, hypercalcemia, and renal dysfunction. Diagnostic criteria require ≥10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus monoclonal protein and myeloma-defining events [ ]. The etiological basis of MM remains incompletely defined, but accumulating evidence indicates a substantial genetic component. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated a 2- to 4-fold increased risk among first-degree relatives of MM patients [ ], supporting inherited susceptibility and motivating investigation into somatic and germline genetic determinants. Over the past two decades, therapeutic advances have transformed MM management. Proteasome inhibitors (PIs) and immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) have improved overall survival (OS) across successive therapeutic eras [ ]. Current treatment paradigms favor combination regimens integrating PIs and IMiDs for newly diagnosed disease. MM is therefore increasingly managed as a chronic, although still incurable, malignancy. Despite this progress, MM remains largely incurable, mainly due to intrinsic and acquired drug resistance. Clinical and molecular studies show that relapse in nearly universal. Therapeutic refractoriness drives progression and mortality [ ]. At the biological level, resistance arises from multiple mechanisms, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, defective apoptotic signaling, immune system dysregulation, and protective interactions between malignant plasma cells and the bone marrow microenvironment [ ]. High-throughput molecular profiling has improved the characterization of resistance mechanisms and strengthened risk stratification, supporting biologically informed treatment selection and the development of mechanism-based therapeutic strategies [ ]. Altogether, these advances support biomarker-driven, risk-adapted therapeutic strategies [ ]. While previous reviews have typically addressed germline susceptibility and somatic evolution in MM as separate domains, or have focused on static descriptions of genomic alterations, this work advances an integrated evolutionary genomics framework that conceptualizes disease initiation and progression as a continuous, multilayered process shaped by inherited genetic background, early clonal selection, and therapy-driven dynamics. By moving beyond a binary germline-versus-somatic perspective, this apporach captures the temporal and biological continuity underlying progression from precursor states to symptomatic disease. Importantly, it provides a clinically oriented scaffold for integrating emerging approaches, such as polygenic risk scores and subclonal reconstruction, into unified models for risk stratification, longitudinal disease monitoring, and treatment adaptation. In this way, the proposed framework not only synthesizes existing knowledge but also offers a conceptual basis for translating genomic complexity into actionable precision oncology strategies. In this review, we synthesize current evidence supporting this model and discuss its implications for precision oncology in MM. Risk factors and genetic predisposition Building on the biological and clinical approach outlined above, MM is recognized as a multifactorial disease arising from the combined effects of aging, environmental exposures, precursor disease states, and inherited genetic susceptibility. These factors interact to shape disease initiation, clonal evolution, and clinical heterogeneity. Epidemiological and molecular studies have identified several determinants that modulate individual risk of disease initiation, progression, and clinical presentation. Together, these determinants inform risk stratification and screening strategies. Environmental and clinical risk factors Demographic and population-level determinants Age represents the strongest independent risk factor for MM. Incidence rises sharply after age 50, peaking around 65, consistent with cumulative mutational burden and immune aging. Forecast models project a marked rise in incident cases over the coming decades. Age is therefore a fundamental component of risk stratification, particularly for screening and early intervention in precursor conditions. Notably, although age is strongly associated with disease incidence, evidence regarding its relationship with specific genomic subtypes remains conflicting. Some studies have reported a higher frequency of IgH translocations, particularly t(4;14), in older patients [ ], whereas others have observed lower rates of these high-risk events in elderly-onset disease, together with distinct mutational profiles and fewer MYC rearrangements [ ]. Consistent sex-related differences in MM incidence have been reported across population registries, with a modest but reproducible male predominance observed worldwide [ ]. Male-to-female incidence ratios range between 1.2:1 and 1.5:1 across diverse geographic regions [ ]. Large population-based datasets confirm that approximately 55–57% of cases occur in men [ ]. MM exhibits significant racial disparities, with African Americans experiencing approximately twice the incidence observed in white populations [ ]. Greenberg et al. proposed that this disparity reflects a higher prevalence of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) rather than increased malignant progression [ ]. This interpretation is supported by more recent large-scale analyses, which show no evidence of differences in progression rates from MGUS to MM across racial groups, indicating that disparities are primarily driven by differences in disease initiation [ ]. These findings reinforce a model in which population-level differences in MGUS prevalence, rather than accelerated progression, account for the higher incidence observed in individuals of African ancestry. Population-level differences have also been described in Chinese cohorts, where patients are diagnosed at a younger median age (∼59 years) and often present with higher disease burden [ ]. Genomic analyses suggest partially distinct mutational landscapes compared with Western cohorts, including differences in NF-κB pathway alterations [ ]. The biological basis of these demographic disparities remains incompletely defined. Age also modifies prognosis. Increasing age is associated with inferior progression-free survival (PFS) and OS [ ]. Age-stratified genomic analyses indicate shifts in lesion frequency, including distribution of high-risk IgH translocations and gain(1q) across age groups [ ], supporting partially distinct evolutionary trajectories in elderly-onset disease. Taken together, age, sex, and ancestry define a foundational demographic risk framework in MM. These variables inform population-level risk estimation and screening strategies. Precursor conditions Virtually all cases of MM are preceded by asymptomatic precursor conditions, primarily MGUS or smoldering MM (SMM). Epidemiological evidence indicates that MGUS affects approximately 3.2% of individuals older than 50 years, with an average annual progression rate to MM of about 1% [ ]. Progression risk is strongly influenced by monoclonal protein burden, bone marrow infiltration, and genetic background [ ]. SMM is associated with a substantially elevated risk of progression to overt MM, particularly during the first five years following diagnosis [ ]. Solitary plasmacytoma also carries a significant risk of progression to systemic disease. These precursor states define biologically and clinically identifiable high-risk populations. Environmental, occupational, lifestyle and clinical modifiers Environmental and occupational exposures are associated with MM susceptibility in multiple epidemiological studies. Meta-analyses report elevated risk in selected occupational groups, including firefighters, who exhibit nearly a 50% increased risk, and hairdressers, with approximately a 40% higher risk [ ]. Farming populations likewise show elevated incidence, particularly in contexts involving pesticide exposure [ ]. At the exposure level, pesticides, herbicides, organic solvents, and petroleum-derived products have been associated with increased MM risk [ ]. Proposed mechanisms include genotoxic stress, chronic inflammation, and DNA damage. Lifestyle-related factors Lifestyle factors influence MM risk largely through effects on precursor plasma cell disorders, with obesity emerging as the most consistent modifiable contributor. Obesity has been strongly associated with increased MGUS and MM risk, with reported odds ratios in the range of approximately 1.7–2.0 [ , ]. This association likely reflects chronic inflammatory and metabolic dysregulation. Large prospective cohort analyses demonstrate a clear dose-dependent association between body mass index (BMI) and MM incidence, with a 17% increase in risk per 5 kg/m² increment in cumulative average adult BMI and a 28% increase per 5 kg/m² rise in young adult BMI [ ]. Obesity has also been associated with inferior clinical outcomes [ ]. Proposed mechanisms include IGF-1 pathway activation, adipokine imbalance, inflammatory cytokine signaling, and adipocyte-stromal interactions. In contrast, tobacco smoking shows no consistent association with MM incidence in large meta-analyses [ ]. However, heavy exposure has been associated with a 2.26-fold increased likelihood of MGUS [ ]. Physical activity appears to exert a modest protective effect, although associations attenuate after adjustment for BMI [ , ]. Dietary patterns may further modulate susceptibility, with plant-based diets associated with lower MM risk [ ]. Vitamin D deficiency has been linked to poorer clinical outcomes rather than disease initiation [ ]. Clinical and immune-related comorbidities as modifying risk factors Clinical comorbidities and immune-mediated conditions have been investigated as MM risk modifiers, with generally modest and heterogeneous associations. Clinical data further support a biologically relevant interaction between chronic viral infection and plasma cell dyscrasia, including potential modulation of disease progression following antiviral therapy [ ]. Mendelian randomization analyses have identified taxa-specific causal associations, and mechanistic studies suggest that dysbiosis may promote disease progression through immune modulation, nitrogen-recycling pathways, and metabolic crosstalk within the bone marrow microenvironment [ ]. Microbiota composition has been associated with treatment response and minimal residual disease (MRD) status [ ]. Autoimmune diseases have been associated with increased susceptibility to MGUS and MM [ ], supporting a role for chronic immune activation. However, large epidemiological analyses show heterogeneous and generally weak associations. Null or weak associations have been reported for primary Sjögren syndrome [ ], ankylosing spondylitis [ ], and rheumatoid arthritis [ ], while findings in systemic lupus erythematosus are inconsistent. Pernicious anemia and ankylosing spondylitis show the most consistent associations with increased MM risk [ , ]. Interestingly, periodontitis, a chronic oral inflammatory disease, has also been linked to MM risk [ ], suggesting a potential role for systemic inflammatory burden in oncogenesis ( ). Familial aggregation and inherited susceptibility Besides environmental and clinical determinants, inherited genetic susceptibility contributes substantially to MM risk. Evidence from familial aggregation studies, rare germline variant analyses, and large-scale GWAS indicates that both high-impact pathogenic variants and polygenic risk architectures contribute to disease predisposition [ , ]. These data support a complex inherited susceptibility landscape. Familial clustering and epidemiological inheritance A substantial heritable component underlies disease susceptibility, as evidenced by consistent familial clustering patterns and the two- to four-fold increased risk observed among first-degree relatives of affected individuals [ , ]. Germline alterations in DNA repair and genome maintenance pathways, including genes such as TP53 and BRCA1/2 , together with immune regulatory and telomere-associated genes ( DIS3, TNFRSF13B, TREX1, POT1 , and TERT ), have been implicated in familial cases [ , ]. Large cohort studies further demonstrate that pathogenic germline variants in DNA repair pathways are present in approximately 9.1% of sporadic MM cases and up to 18% of familial cases [ ]. Rare pathogenic germline variants Rare pathogenic germline variants (PGVs) are detected in approximately 5–30% of patients with MM, with a higher prevalence in familial and early-onset cases, predominantly affecting genes involved in DDR, telomere maintenance, and immune regulation [ , , ]. High- and moderate-penetrance DDR genes, including TP53 (∼2–3%), PALB2, ATM, CHEK2 , and BRCA1/2 , are identified in 4–7% of unselected cohorts and promote defective homologous recombination and impaired p53-mediated apoptosis [ ], thereby accelerating genomic instability. Recurrent alterations in telomere-related genes such as POT1 and TERT , observed in approximately 2–5% of familial MM cases, promote chromosomal fragility and clonal evolution, mirroring mechanisms described in other malignancies [ ]. Variants in immune and B-cell regulatory genes, including TNFRSF13B / TACI and DIS3 , occur in approximately 3–15% of patients and disrupt plasma cell maturation and immune surveillance [ , , ] ( ). Clinically, PGVs are associated with younger age at diagnosis, increased familial cancer burden, and differential therapeutic responses, with drug-response associations reported for selected DDR alterations. Targeted enrichment strategies report higher PGV detection rates, supporting risk-adapted screening algorithms [ ]. Polygenic susceptibility and GWAS architecture Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) meta-analyses have identified >20 susceptibility loci, implicating regulatory networks in immune response, plasma cell differentiation, autophagy, apoptosis, and cell cycle control [ , ]. Inherited risk is predominantly polygenic, driven by cumulative low-penetrance variants [ , ]. Polymorphisms in telomerase-related genes, particularly TERT , further link telomere biology to susceptibility [ ]. Expanded meta-analyses identified additional loci enriched in regulatory regions controlling B-cell differentiation [ ]. Trans-ancestry studies identified shared susceptibility loci at 7p15.3, 17p11.2, and 22q13.1 across African and European ancestry populations, while an additional locus at 3p22.1 showed significant association exclusively in EA cohorts [ ]. Despite these promising findings, PRS are not yet clinically actionable for screening high-risk individuals or relatives in MM, and their implementation in routine practice remains constrained by several key limitations [ , ]. First, PRS models have not been prospectively validated in large, independent cohorts, limiting confidence in their real-world performance and clinical generalizability. In the context of MM, this limitation is particularly relevant given the relatively low disease incidence and the lack of prospective screening approaches in asymptomatic populations. In addition, predictive accuracy is reduced in ancestrally diverse populations, reflecting both the underrepresentation of non-European populations in GWAS and population-specific genetic architectures [ ]. Furthermore, there are no standardized thresholds to define clinically meaningful risk categories, and it remains unclear how PRS-based stratification should be integrated with established MM risk factors such as MGUS status, family history, and cytogenetic markers. As a result, PRS should currently be considered research tools rather than validated instruments for population screening or risk assessment in relatives. Future efforts should focus on prospective validation, cross-population calibration, and integration with somatic genomic features and clinical variables to develop more robust and clinically actionable risk prediction models. However, several limitations constrain the interpretation and translational impact of GWAS findings. Most studies are heavily biased toward populations of European ancestry, limiting generalizability and potentially exacerbating disparities in risk prediction [ , ]. Moreover, the effect sizes of individual susceptibility variants are modest, and the biological mechanisms linking many loci to MM pathogenesis remain incompletely defined, as many GWAS signals map to regulatory regions with context-dependent functional effects [ ]. Importantly, currently identified susceptibility loci explain only a fraction of the heritable risk of MM, with large-scale interaction analyses estimating that known variants and their interactions account for approximately 17% of heritability, highlighting a substantial component of “missing heritability” [ , ]. Reproducibility across cohorts is also variable, reflecting differences in study design, sample size, statistical power, and phenotype definition. In addition, comparative analyses across studies reveal partial overlap in identified loci, but also inconsistencies in effect sizes and significance levels, highlighting the influence of cohort composition and analytical pipelines. Importantly, GWAS approaches primarily capture common variants and do not adequately account for rare high-impact mutations, structural variation, or epigenetic regulation, thereby providing only a partial view of inherited risk architecture. These limitations are further underscored by sequencing-based studies, which have identified rare pathogenic variants and additional layers of genetic complexity not captured by GWAS approaches [ , ]. Furthermore, conflicting evidence exists regarding the functional relevance of several susceptibility loci, with limited experimental validation and uncertainty about their contribution to disease biology. Although gene–gene interaction analyses have identified a limited number of interacting loci, the overall contribution of epistatic effects remains incompletely resolved, and robust replication across independent cohorts is still lacking. Gene–environment interactions are even less well characterized, representing a major unresolved area in MM susceptibility research. Addressing these challenges will require larger multi-ancestry cohorts, integrative multi-omic approaches, functional validation of candidate loci, and standardized analytical frameworks to improve robustness, biological interpretation, and clinical applicability [ , , ]. Genetic-environment interactions Genetic-environment interactions constitute another layer of MM etiology, where inherited susceptibility amplifies the biological impact of environmental exposures. Rare germline variants affecting DNA damage response, telomere maintenance, and immune pathways may increase cellular vulnerability to genotoxic stressors [ ]. Occupational exposure to pesticides and solvents has been associated with increased MM risk, and may exert stronger biological effects in individuals carrying germline alterations in DNA repair pathways [ ]. Germline alterations in DNA repair genes and immune regulators increase cellular sensitivity to genotoxic stressors including pesticides, solvents, and benzene, accelerating mutational accumulation, inflammatory signaling, and clonal evolution during progression from MGUS and SMM to MM [ , ]. Obesity may further synergize with polygenic risk through chronic inflammation and metabolic reprogramming of the bone marrow microenvironment [ ]. In genetically predisposed individuals, these inflammatory and metabolic pressures may facilitate earlier clonal expansion and disease progression. High-resolution longitudinal cohort efforts integrating exposure data, clonal hematopoiesis dynamics, and molecular profiling further support the role of G × E interactions in shaping disease trajectories and provide a foundation for personalized prevention and surveillance strategies in high-risk populations [ ]. Somatic genomic landscape of MM Primary cytogenetic abnormalities represent early detectable genomic events in MM and define major biological subtypes. These lesions arise during premalignant stages, persist throughout clonal evolution, and shape downstream mutational trajectories, clinical behavior, and therapeutic vulnerability. Two largely mutually exclusive categories account for most cases: recurrent immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) chromosomal translocations and hyperdiploidy. Together, these categories define distinct evolutionary routes and underpin cytogenetic risk stratification. Primary cytogenetic categories Primary cytogenetic events define early MM subtypes and shape genomic evolution. IgH-driven translocations • IgH translocations as early genomic drivers and their clinical detection Chromosome 14q32 rearrangements involving the IgH locus represent one of the most frequent and relevant primary genomic events in MM [ ]. These alterations arise early during disease progression, are detectable in MGUS, and generally persist during progression, while secondary alterations such as MYC activation and TP53 loss accumulate later [ ]. At the functional level, IgH translocations juxtapose oncogenes to the highly active IgH enhancer region, leading to deregulated expression of genes involved in cell cycle control, epigenetic regulation, transcriptional programs, and survival. IgH rearrangements are detected in approximately 40–50% of NDMM patients using conventional techniques [ , ], and may approach 50–60% with comprehensive genomic profiling. • Dominant IgH translocation subtypes and biological consequences Four chromosomal partners account for the majority of primary IgH translocations: CCND1 (11q13), CCND3 (6p21), FGFR3/WHSC1 (MMSET) (4p16), and MAF (16q23) [ ]. The t(11;14)(q13;q32), present in approximately 15–20% of patients [ , ], drives CCND1 overexpression [ ] and is associated with a lymphoplasmacytic phenotype, frequent CD20 expression, and relative biological indolence [ ]. This subgroup is generally classified as standard risk [ ]. Tumors with t(11;14) show relative dependence on BCL2-mediated survival pathways, which is associated with increased response rates to venetoclax-based strategies in selected patient subsets [ ]. The t(4;14)(p16.3;q32), observed in approximately 10–15% of cases [ ], results in simultaneous activation of FGFR3 and WHSC1 (MMSET) [ ]. MMSET overexpression alters chromatin methylation and DNA damage response pathways [ ], while FGFR3 contributes oncogenic signaling in a subset of patients harboring activating mutations, detected in approximately 17% of t(4;14)-positive tumors [ ]. This subgroup defines a high-risk entity characterized by aggressive clinical behavior, frequent renal involvement, and inferior survival [ ]. PI-based therapy partially mitigates adverse prognosis, highlighting the therapeutic relevance of molecular stratification [ ]. The t(14;16)(q32;q23), present in approximately 2–3% of patients [ ], induces MAF overexpression and has been associated with inferior survival [ , ]. MAF activation promotes APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B expression, generating a hypermutator phenotype characterized by APOBEC mutational signatures and increased genomic instability [ ]. Less frequent primary events include t(6;14) (1–2%), associated with CCND3 activation and generally neutral prognosis [ ], and t(14;20) (∼1%), associated with MAFB activation and adverse prognosis in overt MM [ ]. Hyperdiploidy In parallel to IgH-driven disease, hyperdiploidy represents the second major primary cytogenetic category in MM and accounts for approximately 45–50% of NDMM cases in Western populations [ , ]. It is defined by non-random gain of odd-numbered chromosomes, most commonly involving chromosomes 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 19, and 21. These gains are acquired in structured evolutionary sequences rather than through random aneuploidy, defining a distinct early oncogenic route. Reported incidence varies across cohorts, likely reflecting technical and population differences [ , ]. It is defined by non-random gain of odd-numbered chromosomes, most commonly involving chromosomes 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 19, and 21. These gains are acquired in structured evolutionary sequences rather than through random aneuploidy, defining a distinct early oncogenic route. Reported incidence varies across cohorts, likely reflecting technical and population differences [ , ]. Among patients with cytogenetically abnormal karyotypes, hyperdiploidy is the most frequent numerical pattern, occurring in approximately 46–68% of cases, compared with pseudodiploid or hypodiploid configurations. From a clinical perspective, patients with abnormal metaphase karyotypes exhibit inferior survival outcomes compared with those with normal karyotypes [ ]. Hyperdiploid MM is associated with more favorable survival compared with hypodiploid disease, defined by fewer than 45 chromosomes [ ], indicating that numerical chromosomal patterns differ in impact. Prognostic impact is heterogeneous. Patients with hyperdiploidy plus high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities, including del(17p13), t(4;14), and gain of 1q21, experience significantly worse survival outcomes than patients with isolated hyperdiploidy [ ]. Chromosome-specific effects further modulate prognosis within the hyperdiploid subgroup. Among hyperdiploid patients, only trisomy 3 and trisomy 5 were independently associated with improved OS, whereas trisomy 21 correlated with adverse clinical outcomes [ , ], indicating that trisomy pattern, not chromosome count alone, influences prognosis. Secondary genomic events and progression-associated events Secondary genomic events shape MM progression biology and include chromosome-arm aneuploidy, focal CNVs, and secondary structural alterations that accumulate on primary cytogenetic backgrounds. Aneuploidy-driven/trigger progression in MM With the advent of high-resolution molecular cytogenetic techniques, studies show that 95–100% of patients with MM harbor abnormal karyotypes, often characterized by highly complex combinations of structural and numerical alterations. Early comparative genomic hybridization and FISH-based studies established that these alterations are nonrandom and biologically selected. Reported recurrent chromosome-arm gains involving 19p, 9q, 11q, 12q, 15q, 17q, and 22q, together with deletions affecting 6q and 16q. Subsequent interphase FISH analyses confirmed chromosomal aberrations in up to 86% of NDMM patients, with frequent gains of chromosomes 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, and 21 and losses involving chromosomes 13 and 17, and identified del(13q14) and IGH translocations as major prognostic markers [ ]. gain At the chromosome-arm level, gain of 1q is the most frequent and clinically relevant numerical event. It occurs in approximately 35–40% of NDMM patients and increases in frequency at relapse, where it strongly correlates with treatment resistance and inferior survival [ , ]. Prognostic impact appears to be copy-number dependent, with ≥4 copies generally associated with inferior outcomes compared with three copies, although this association is influenced by co-existing cytogenetic abnormalities and contemporary treatment strategies [ ]. Notably, the prognostic effect of +1q/1q21 gains is not uniform across studies: in thalidomide-based regimens no significant survival impact has been reported, and in other series the adverse association observed in univariate analyses did not retain independent prognostic value in multivariable models [ ]. deletion Deletion of chromosome 1p is detected in approximately 27–30% of patients and represents another major adverse lesion [ ]. del(1p) is independently associated with poor prognosis [ , , ]. Of particular biological relevance are deletions involving 1p12 and 1p32.3, regions that harbor critical tumor suppressor candidates. del(13q) Deletion of chromosome 13q occurs in approximately 50–60% of patients [ , ]. Its adverse prognostic signal largely reflects co-occurrence with other high-risk lesions. del(17p) Deletion of chromosome 17p involving the TP53 represents the most clinically impactful arm-level abnormality. Del(17p) is detected in approximately 8–10% of NDMM patients and is consistently associated with inferior PFS and OS [ , ]. Its prevalence increases dramatically during disease progression, reaching very high frequencies in advanced and relapsed stages [ , ]. TP53 functions as a central regulator of cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis, and 17p loss is associated with aggressive disease, inferior OS, and increased risk of extramedullary involvement [ , , ]. Other arm-level gains/losses Additional recurrent arm-level gains include gains of 8q, 9q, and 11q, with 8q gain of particular relevance due to the MYC locus at 8q24 [ , , ]. Recurrent arm-level losses include 1p, 6q, 8p, 9q, 13q, 16q, and 17p, contributing to tumor suppressor gene depletion and genomic imbalance [ , , ]. Several of these losses co-occur with gain(1q), defining broader chromosomal instability patterns. MYC secondary events Dysregulation of MYC represents a central secondary genomic event in MM progression [ ]. Unlike primary IgH translocations, MYC rearrangements are rare in premalignant stages (3–4%) [ ], but increase in frequency in NDMM (approximately 15–20%) [ , , ] and become further enriched at relapse, where they are associated with proliferative transcriptional programs and inferior clinical outcomes [ , ]. Recurrent MYC rearrangements, focal gains, and amplifications involving 8q24 constitute multiple structural mechanisms converging

MYC secondary events Dysregulation of MYC represents a central secondary genomic event in MM progression [ ]. Unlike primary IgH translocations, MYC rearrangements are rare in premalignant stages (3–4%) [ ], but increase in frequency in NDMM (approximately 15–20%) [ , , ] and become further enriched at relapse, where they are associated with proliferative transcriptional programs and inferior clinical outcomes [ , ]. Recurrent MYC rearrangements, focal gains, and amplifications involving 8q24 constitute multiple structural mechanisms converging on MYC activation [ , ]. These alterations are particularly enriched in tumors with homologous recombination deficiency and show an inverse correlation with t(4;14) [ , ]. Their frequent coexistence with primary IgH translocations supports a multistep evolutionary model of myeloma progression. Functionally, MYC activation drives proliferative transcriptional programs contributing to clonal diversification, adverse clinical behavior and progression [ , ]. The stepwise increase in MYC alterations from MGUS to symptomatic and relapsed MM reinforces its role as a progression-associated lesion rather than an initiating event. Driver-focused copy number remodeling Building on the arm-level architecture described above, focal CNVs modulate oncogenic dosage and functional heterogeneity without defining new cytogenetic categories. Recurrent amplifications and deletions target gene-dense regions that modulate key oncogenic pathways. Representative events include focal amplification of CKS1B (1q21) and MYC (8q24), deletions involving TP53 (17p13), CDKN2C and FAF1 (1p32), RB1 (13q14), CYLD (16q12), and BIRC2/BIRC3 (11q22), converging on cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage response, and NF-κB signaling [ , ]. Focal CNVs interact with aneuploid backgrounds to promote transcriptional reprogramming, clonal fitness, and therapeutic resistance. Integrated analyses associate specific CNV patterns with aggressive transcriptional states and inferior survival (Gupta et al., 2019). Longitudinal studies further show CNV remodeling under therapeutic pressure, fostering branched clonal evolution and resistance [ ]. CNV remodeling frequently coexists with complex structural variation, reinforcing genomic instability and hierarchical evolution [ ] ( ). Genomic detection strategies: from FISH to NGS and optical genome mapping (OGM) Accurate identification of myeloma genomic abnormalities is central for risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making. Conventional diagnostic workflows rely on fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), SNP arrays, targeted sequencing, and OGM, typically requiring plasma cell enrichment for optimal sensitivity. Conventional cytogenetics and FISH Conventional metaphase cytogenetics and interphase FISH remain central to MM diagnosis and risk stratification, forming the backbone of current clinical guidelines. FISH, performed on plasma cell-enriched samples, overcomes the low proliferative index that limits metaphase analysis and reliably detects high-risk lesions such as t(4;14), t(14;16), del(17p), 1q gain, and 1p deletion [ ]. Detection rates consistently exceed those of conventional cytogenetics: abnormalities were identified in 49.2% versus 16.9% of cases in one cohort [ ], and up to 97% versus 30% when FISH combined with array-CGH was compared with karyotyping alone [ ]. Beyond detection, FISH allows estimation of lesion burden and subclonal distribution, guiding risk-adapted therapy. Conventional cytogenetics, although less sensitive, retains complementary value by providing a global view of ploidy and chromosomal complexity, including hyperdiploidy and complex karyotypes [ ]. NGS-based structural variant detection NGS extends structural variant detection beyond predefined probe panels. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and targeted sequencing approaches can identify cryptic rearrangements, resolve complex breakpoints, and uncover novel fusion partners [ ]. Panel design remains critical, as limited genomic coverage may underestimate clinically relevant alterations, including certain MYC rearrangements. Beyond structural rearrangements, NGS enables simultaneous detection of single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels), particularly relevant for TP53 , where focal deletions frequently coexist with inactivating mutations. NGS sensitivity depends on sequencing depth and variant allele fraction; high-depth sequencing achieves >98% sensitivity for SNVs and indels [ ]. Integrated WES/RNA-seq demonstrate complete concordance with FISH for CNAs while additionally resolving translocation breakpoints and mutations [ ]. High-performance custom panels also show >99% sensitivity for IGH translocations and CNVs [ ]. Collectively, these findings support integrated NGS-cytogenetic strategies, as NGS captures structural variants and sequence mutations, providing gene-level profiling beyond conventional cytogenetics. Optical genome mapping (OGM) Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) enables detection of structural variants, CNVs, and aneuploidy in a single experiment, overcoming the locus restriction of targeted FISH panels. Across clinical cohorts, OGM identifies canonical abnormalities detectable by FISH while revealing additional structural variants. One study reported a ∼30% increase in prognostic yield compared with FISH [ ], whereas another detected additional alterations in up to 60% of cases, including chromoanagenesis events [ ]. High concordance with FISH for variants ≥5% with a variant allele frequency supports reliability for major clonal events [ ]. By capturing balanced rearrangements and numerical changes in a single workflow, OGM functions as a high-resolution digital karyotype and may consolidate multiple cytogenetic assays. However, OGM sensitivity decreases for low-level subclones (15–20%) and it cannot reliably resolve centromeric or telomeric

By capturing balanced rearrangements and numerical changes in a single workflow, OGM functions as a high-resolution digital karyotype and may consolidate multiple cytogenetic assays. However, OGM sensitivity decreases for low-level subclones (15–20%) and it cannot reliably resolve centromeric or telomeric rearrangements [ ]. Performance may be reduced in samples with low plasma cell purity or highly subclonal populations. In addition, OGM requires ultra-high molecular weight DNA, which can be challenging to obtain from bone marrow samples. Importantly, OGM does not detect SNVs or small insertions/deletions [ ], and therefore requires integration with sequencing platforms for comprehensive profiling. Prognostic implications and therapeutic modulation Cytogenetic abnormalities are the strongest predictors of clinical outcome. Deletion 17p, t(4;14), and 1q21 gain are independent adverse prognostic factors for PFS, with del(17p13) also predicting inferior OS [ ]. Cytogenetic complexity further worsens prognosis. High-dose therapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation improves response depth but does not fully offset high-risk cytogenetic features. In contrast, incorporation of PI shows particular benefit in t(4;14) and 1q21 gain disease, supporting molecularly risk-adapted therapy [ , ]. Mutational profiles and clonal evolution High-resolution chromatin conformation studies show that CNV breakpoints frequently occur at the boundaries of topologically associating domains (TADs), suggesting preferential disruption of regulatory regions. TADs organize the genome into insulated neighborhoods that constrain enhancer-promoter interactions and shape gene expression programs [ ]. TAD disruption alters enhancer-promoter interactions and contributes to oncogenic dysregulation [ ]. Compared with normal B cells, MM shows increased TAD number, reduced average TAD size, and A/B compartment switching in ∼20% of genomic regions, consistent with higher-order genome reorganization [ , ] ( ). Comparative genomic studies indicate that MGUS is genetically related to MM but exhibits a lower burden of genomic abnormalities. The frequency of chromosomal gains and losses, including hyperdiploidy, 1q gain, and del(13q), is reduced in MGUS, supporting a stepwise accumulation of genomic instability during progression. MGUS also shows a less complex somatic mutation spectrum that correlates with chromosomal and mutational burden [ ]. MYC translocations and TP53 lesions are typically absent in MGUS, supporting their role as transformation-associated events. Large sequencing cohorts demonstrate that progression is accompanied by diversification of mutational processes affecting both coding and non-coding regions. Analysis of CoMMpass whole-exome and whole-genome datasets identified recurrent SNVs, structural rearrangements, and characteristic mutational signatures linked to endogenous enzymatic activity and therapy-related mutagenesis [ , ]. Integrated genomic analyses combining sequencing, CNV profiling, and cytogenetics describe linear, branching, and parallel evolutionary trajectories, highlighting dynamic clonal architecture [ , ]. In MM, subclonal architecture can be reconstructed from bulk NGS data using probabilistic frameworks based on Bayesian clustering of variant allele frequencies and copy-number–adjusted cancer cell fractions. These approaches model the contribution of individual mutations to the overall tumor population, accounting for tumor purity and local copy number, and group variants into clusters that reflect distinct clonal populations. In particular, Dirichlet-process-based models enable data-driven inference of the number and composition of subclonal populations without requiring prior specification of cluster number [ , ]. This allows the identification of phylogenetically related clones and the distinction between truncal and branch mutations, providing a basis for reconstructing tumor evolutionary histories. These approaches have been applied in longitudinal and progression settings to track clonal dynamics over time and under therapeutic pressure, revealing that subclonal diversity often precedes clinical transformation and that relapse may arise from pre-existing minor clones [ , , ]. However, despite their relevance, their implementation in routine clinical practice remains limited by the lack of standardized bioinformatic pipelines, methodological variability across tools, and the intrinsic constraints of bulk sequencing data. The development of robust and standardized analytical approaches will be essential to fully integrate subclonal resolution into precision oncology strategies. An additional layer of complexity arises from allele-specific expression of somatic variants. Transcriptomic profiling shows that mutant alleles are variably expressed, with selective activation or silencing that modulates functional impact beyond DNA sequence alone [ ]. At the pathway level, somatic mutations are enriched in receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and cell adhesion networks. Sequencing of tumors and myeloma cell lines identified recurrent alterations affecting plasma cell adhesion, migration, and microenvironmental interactions [ ]. Germline susceptibility variants may further modulate the risk and molecular progression of plasma cell dyscrasias. At relapse, genomic complexity increases. Integrative analyses show more chromosomal imbalances at relapse than at diagnosis, driven mainly by additional losses, with recurrent relapse-associated gains on 8q and losses of 10q [ , , ]. Large CNVs (>100 Mb) exert stronger transcriptional effects than smaller alterations and preferentially deregulate cytokine-related and integrin signaling pathways. Relapse-associated expression changes include activation of PRAME (22q11) and BOP1 (8q24). Global DNA methylation patterns remain relatively stable between diagnosis and relapse, indicating a dominant role for chromosomal remodeling over epigenetic reprogramming in late-stage progression [ ]. Germline genetic susceptibility GWAS As mentioned above, GWAS have established that MM has a substantial inherited component driven by a polygenic architecture. Numerous common low-penetrance variants collectively contribute to disease susceptibility. Large-scale meta-analyses indicate that germline risk loci explain approximately 20–25% of heritable risk, confirming that genetic predisposition arises from the cumulative effect of multiple regulatory variants rather than rare high-penetrance alleles. GWAS therefore provide direct molecular evidence of inherited susceptibility beyond familial aggregation. International collaborations such as IMMEnSE were instrumental to power discovery and cross-cohort validation [ ]. A landmark meta-analysis conducted by Mitchell et al. analyzed 9866 cases and 239,188 controls. This study validated nine previously reported susceptibility loci and identified eight additional risk regions. Newly implicated loci included JARID2 (6p22.3), ATG5 (6q21), SMARCD3 (7q36.1), CCAT1 (8q24.21), CDKN2A (9p21.3), WAC (10p12.1), RFWD3 (16q23.1), and PREX1 (20q13.13) [ ]. Earlier GWAS also identified additional loci, including a variant at 2q12.3 associated with increased MM risk and replicated across multiple cohorts [ ]. Trans-ethnic GWAS approaches further refined inherited MM risk architecture by leveraging ancestry-specific linkage disequilibrium (LD) structure, which is particularly relevant given higher incidence in individuals of African ancestry. Rand et al. combined European and African ancestry cohorts and replicated several established European risk loci at CDCA7L (7p15.3), TNFRSF13B (17p11.2), and CBX7 (22q13.1). They also improved fine-mapping of shared susceptibility regions using ancestry-specific LD patterns [ ]. The expanded African ancestry meta-analysis by Du et al. showed concordant risk architecture across populations while identifying ancestry-dependent effect sizes [ ]. More recently, Went et al. reported that multi-ancestry PRS identify the highest predicted genetic risk in admixed American populations, partly driven by enrichment of risk alleles at loci such as 3p22.1 near ULK4 [ ]. Beyond single-locus associations, pathway-based and interaction analyses reveal higher-order genetic dependencies. Polygenic interaction modeling of two independent GWAS datasets identified 16 significant interacting variant pairs, supporting a contribution of epistatic effects to inherited MM risk [ ]. Independent replication studies further confirmed additional susceptibility loci, including variants at 8q24, 7p15.3, 3p22.1, and 2p23.3 [ , , ]. Functionally, many GWAS risk variants localize to non-coding regulatory regions and act through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mechanisms in hematopoietic tissues. Risk loci cluster near genes involved in plasma cell differentiation and immune signaling, including TNFRSF13B / TACI and PREX1 . Integration of transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) has prioritized >100 candidate susceptibility genes, including APOBEC -family members, linking inherited risk to mutational processes relevant to somatic progression in MM. Importantly, aggregation of GWAS signals into PRS enables population-level susceptibility stratification, with individuals in the highest percentiles exhibiting a significantly increased relative risk. Trans-ethnic modeling improves PRS portability across ancestries and supports more equitable risk prediction strategies. Candidate gene association studies Candidate gene association studies have evaluated inherited variants in pathways related to drug transport, DNA repair, autophagy, immune regulation, plasma cell differentiation, microenvironmental signaling and telomere maintenance. Reported associations span susceptibility, clinical features, treatment outcomes and comorbidities [ , , , ] ( ). Xenobiotic transport and drug metabolism (ABC, GST) ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are key xenobiotic efflux pumps that contribute to multidrug resistance in MM. They export chemotherapeutic agents from malignant plasma cells, thereby reducing intracellular drug accumulation. Major transporters implicated include ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein/ MDR1 ), ABCC1 ( MRP1 ), ABCC5 ( MRP5 ), and ABCG2 ( BCRP ), frequently upregulated in relapsed and refractory disease. Increased transporter expression is frequently driven by epigenetic demethylation and microenvironment-derived signaling pathways, including resistin-mediated NF-κB activation. These mechanisms collectively promote cross-resistance. Polymorphisms in xenobiotic transport and detoxification genes have been investigated as modifiers of treatment response and outcome. Early studies reported that GSTM1 and GSTT1 deletions did not significantly influence response or survival in NDMM patients treated with vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone (VAD) or high-dose melphalan [ ]. Similarly, Schilthuizen et al. analyzed CYP3A4, CYP3A5, MDR1, GSTM1 , and GSTT1 variants in 209 NDMM patients and found no significant associations with outcome or toxicity [ ]. In contrast, data from the MRC VII trial showed that the GSTP1 Val/Val genotype was associated with improved outcome in patients receiving conventional chemotherapy-based regimens [ ], suggesting context-dependent pharmacogenetic effects. Genetic variation in MDR1 (ABCB1) has also been associated with differential outcomes. Xiao et al. reported that the T allele at C1236T was associated with longer PFS than CC homozygotes, and the T allele at C3435T was associated with longer PFS than CC, with no significant OS association [ ]. Larger multicenter analyses from the IMMEnSE consortium identified survival associations for ABCB1 and ABCC2 variants [ ], supporting a role of transporter polymorphism in therapy modulation rather than baseline susceptibility [ ]. ABCC2 overexpression has also been linked to increased drug clearance and resistance [ ]. In contrast, a meta-analysis of MDR1 rs1045642 (C > T) across four case-control studies found no association with disease susceptibility, consistent with a predominant role in therapy modulation rather than baseline risk [ ]. DNA damage response and genomic stability Genomic instability is a defining feature of MM and reflects alterations in DDR pathways that promote clonal evolution and therapeutic resistance. Both intrinsic repair defects and microenvironmental modulation contribute to altered DDR dynamics [ , ]. Bone marrow niche-derived signals modulate DDR activation and repair capacity, reinforcing instability and therapy resistance [ ]. DDR signaling is frequently compromised. Alterations in checkpoint regulators such as ATM and TP53 blunt apoptotic responses, allowing unstable clones to persist [ ]. Compensatory activation of specific repair modules may further sustain survival under genotoxic stress [ ]. The microenvironment amplifies instability through hypoxia, oxidative stress, inflammatory cytokines, and stromal-derived factors that increase DNA damage and influence DDR pathway choice [ ]. Epigenetic regulators also modulate DDR control. SIRT6 regulates DNA damage signaling and genome stability, and elevated expression correlates with adverse outcomes and resistance to DNA-damaging agents [ ]. Immune regulation and inflammatory pathways (NLRP3, NF-κB, cytokines) Dysregulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway has been described in MM, with reduced NLRP3 and caspase-1 in marrow plasma cells accompanied by elevated circulating IL-18 and altered sRANKL/OPG ratios [ ]. Inflammasome activation also extends beyond malignant plasma cells, as β2-microglobulin induces NLRP3 activation in tumor-associated macrophages, increasing IL-1β/IL-18 and promoting progression [ ]. Polymorphisms in inflammasome-related genes, particularly CARD8 - C10X (rs2043211), have been associated with MM susceptibility and immune-related clinical characteristics [ ], while variants in NF-κb1 (rs28362491) and IL-18 (rs16944) correlated with tumor burden parameters [ ]. Meta-analyses further report associations between IL-6, IL-1 , and IL-10 polymorphisms and MM susceptibility [ ]. Although peripheral T helper subsets are implicated in MM biology, associations with inflammasome polymorphisms appear limited [ ], indicating that inflammatory dysregulation may be compartment-restricted. Plasma cell differentiation and transcriptional regulation (ELL2, IRF4 axis) Functional characterization of germline susceptibility loci provides mechanistic insight into inherited risk. Li et al. identified rs6877329 as a functional variant at 5q15, showing disruption of a B cell-specific enhancer ∼35 kb upstream of ELL2 that loops to the ELL2 promoter [ ]. The rs6877329-C risk allele reduces enhancer activity and was associated with decreased ELL2 expression in CD138⁺ plasma cells, supported by eQTL analyses, and this effect was lineage-restricted with no detectable effect in non-plasma cell compartments. Park et al. showed that ELL2 drives secretory mRNA production and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) in plasma cells [ ]. Reduced ELL2 expression therefore links regulatory variation to impaired differentiation and risk of transformation. Angiogenesis and microenvironment modulators (VEGF/VEGFR) Angiogenesis contributes to MM pathogenesis and prognosis, and increased marrow microvessel density is associated with unfavorable outcomes, supporting the rationale for targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling [ ]. Genetic variation within the VEGF signaling axis modulates angiogenic activity and response to thalidomide-based regimens. The ACG haplotype composed of rs699947, rs833061, and rs2010963, associated with increased VEGF production, was linked to shorter time to thalidomide failure in relapsed MM and shorter time to next treatment in thalidomide-treated NDMM cohorts [ ]. At the tissue level, VEGF rs1570360GG carriers showed higher bone marrow microvessel density [ ]. Polymorphisms in VEGF and VEGFR2 have been associated with treatment response and with disease risk and aggressiveness in case-control analyses [ ]. HLA polymorphisms and immune surveillance Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules mediate immune surveillance by presenting antigenic peptides to T-cell receptors. HLA class I/II polymorphisms shape peptide-binding repertoires and influence immune recognition thresholds [ ]. In MM, inherited HLA variation has been implicated in disease susceptibility and immune control [ ]. GWAS identified HLA-DRB501 as risk allele tagging the classical HLA-DRB101:01 [ ]. In addition, HLA-C07:02 g and HLA-B07:02 g were also reported as independent susceptibility factors, supporting contributions from both class I and class II molecules. HLA class I variation may also influence NK-cell regulation through KIR interactions, thereby influencing immune surveillance [ ]. Beelen et al. reported that a C1-/C2+/Bw4+ epitope combination was associated with MM occurrence, with increased Bw4/KIR3DL1 and C2/KIR2DL1 genotype co-occurrence in MM patients [ ]. Martínez-Sánchez et al. reported that MM risk is associated with less diverse and lower-affinity KIR-HLA-C licensing interactions, a pattern associated with reduced NK responsiveness and potential immune escape [ ]. Therapeutically, inhibitory NK checkpoints restrain anti-myeloma activity, and targeting these pathways may enhance NK cytotoxicity [ ]. Collectively, inherited HLA/KIR variation shapes MM susceptibility and immune control by modulating NK-cell education and effector function. Genetic determinants of therapeutic response in MM Genetic determinants of response to PIs PIs inhibit the proteolytic core of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), a central regulator of protein turnover and signaling homeostasis. By blocking UPS-dependent degradation, proteins accumulate, inducing proteotoxic stress and activation of terminal UPR. This mechanism is particularly relevant in malignant plasma cells, where high immunoglobulin production and genetically driven secretory load create substantial proteostasis stress and intrinsic vulnerability [ ]. Proteasome blockade induces ER stress, immunoglobulin retention, UPR hyperactivation, and disruption of survival transcriptional programs. Experimental data indicate that the magnitude of UPR activation correlates with PI sensitivity, supporting a transcriptional state-dependent response. Response to PIs is heterogeneous and reflects tumor-intrinsic programs and inter-individual modifiers. Tumor genomic architecture can increase protein synthesis, secretory burden, and regulatory instability, elevating proteostasis workload and UPS dependence [ , ]. Next-generation inhibitors differ in subunit selectivity and depth of catalytic blockade, modulating stress-network disruption and response patterns [ , ]. Gene expression-based predictors further support a transcriptionally determined component of PI response [ ]. Germline polymorphisms in proteasome-related genes have been reported, although most signals remain candidate modifiers without clinical validation [ ]. Differences between Btz, carfilzomib (Kfz), and ixazomib (Ixa) reflect distinct subunit engagement and depth of catalytic blockade superimposed on shared UPS dependence. Btz is a reversible β5 subunit inhibitor that perturbs proteostasis and stress-response networks in MM cells. It induces proteotoxic stress, activates the UPR, and modulates NF-κb signaling in a context-dependent manner, targeting genetically constrained survival circuits [ ]. UPR effectors including PERK and ATF4 are rapidly activated. Baseline and inducible expression of UPR regulators such as XBP1, ATF3 , and ATF4 has been associated with differential Btz sensitivity, supporting transcriptional state-dependent response [ , ]. NF-κb effects are context dependent and can include canonical activation, underscoring condition-dependent pathway modulation [ ]. Gene-expression signatures further support drug-class–specific transcriptional determinants of response [ ]. Pharmacogenomic studies suggest that regulatory variation may contribute to response heterogeneity [ ]. Variants in proteasome subunits (e.g., PSMB5, PSMB6, PSMB9) have been associated with differential response in exploratory cohorts, although survival correlations remain inconsistent [ , ].

Subgroup analyses suggest that IRd reduces the hazard of progression versus Rd alone in high-risk patients, indicating partial mitigation of cytogenetic risk rather than full risk neutralization.
